title: Investigating Factors Affecting Oxygen Reduction Reaction on Boron Doped Diamond Electrode and Its Possible Effects on Neural Stimulation
abstract: The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in neural stimulation electrochemically generates reactive oxygen species, which if diffused away into the implanted tissue, might cause tissue damage. Therefore the ORR should be as minimized in neural stimulation (JT.Morton, 1994; S.F Morgan, 2010; EM Hudak, 2017). Boron-doped diamond electrodes have attracted considerable interest as a bio-interfacing electrode material, because of their biocompatibility, wide water window, and electrochemical stability; they also have been reported to have slow kinetics for the ORR. However, few investigations have focused on how its sp 2 carbon content, or non-diamond content, can contribute to oxygen reduction. Moreover, ultranano-crystaline diamond (sp 2 abundant) was recently reported in neural interface applications, justifying the need for further understanding the effect of sp 2 carbon. In this work, we investigate how sp 2 coverage affects the ORR on polycrystalline diamond film electrodes, and also how other factors such as anodic oxidation increase ORR activity. Electrochemical redox activity of Fe 2+/3+ and Raman spectroscopy were used to characterize sp 2 content, and X-ray Photo electron spectroscopy to probe surface oxygen functional groups, before and after anodic oxidation. The electrode’s cathodic charge storage capacity (cCSC), as a measure of the relative contribution of oxygen electrochemistry in charge injection, was compared with cyclic voltammetry (200mV/s scan rate) in N2 and O2 saturated phosphate buffered saline (PBS). Preliminary results showed that diamond electrodes containing surface sp 2 carbon showed more activity towards oxygen reduction than those containing less sp 2 carbon. In addition, we found that if sp 2 containing electrode was anodically oxidized by potential scanning in dilute H 2 SO 4 , the cathodic current (presumably oxygen reduction current) increased. The increase in ORR activity after anodic oxidation could be explained by surface chemistry change or increased surface roughness (thus effective surface area). Since anodic polarization can oxidize an as-grown, primarily hydrogen-terminated diamond surface, and reaching anodic potentials during neural stimulation is inevitable, the effect of anodic oxidation should also be considered when evaluating the effect of sp 2 carbon. In the future, possible products of ORR will be investigated, and the ORR process investigated using faster scan rates to match the time scale of neural stimulation methods.

title: Rheological Study of Natural Starch Biomaterial for Building Biomimetic Immune Tissue
abstract: Mimicking lymph tissue is challenging, yet crucial for understanding cell-mediated immune responses, and translating into clinical immunotherapy treatments. The 3D bioprinting technology is emerging for creating in-vivo like scaffolds as extracellular matrices, allowing spatial arrangement and 3D tissue culture of cells. However, existing bioinks still rely on crosslinkers and chemical modifications to produce printable bioinks, particularly for most biocompatible collagen materials. The chemical crosslink and modifications can introduce toxicity and unwanted cell-matrix interactions. Thus, we proposed the natural starch material to blend with collagen as a novel, non-toxic 3D bioink. We systematically investigated the rheological behavior of starch under different concentrations and gelation heating temperatures. We also studied the mixture ratio with collagen for developing the 3D printability. The optimized rheology is correlated with 3D printing shape fidelity, which leads to a new, non-chemically crosslinked collagen bioink. We also evaluated the biocompatibility of this bioink using MTT assay. The cell viability with our developed bioink scaffold showed good consistency with biocompatible collagen materials. This study introduces a new class of 3D bioink which could advance 3D tissue engineering and facilitate fast growing of immunotherapy treatment strategy.

title: Critical Role of Lipin-2 in the Development of Chronic Multifocal Osteomyelitis
abstract: Chronic Recurrent Multifocal Osteomyelitis (CRMO) is an autoinflammatory bone disorder that causes patients to exhibit chronically active or recurrent sterile bone lesions at multiple sites. The chronic multifocal osteomyelitis (cmo) mouse carries a mutation in the Pstpip2 gene and develops IL-1b mediated sterile bone disorder reminiscent of human CRMO. On the other hand, mutation in the LPIN2 gene that encodes for , a vital molecule in lipid metabolism, is known to cause an autoinflammatory disease called Majeed syndrome which is characterized by CRMO, dyserythropoietic anemia, and may have neutrophilic skin inflammation. Previous reports have shown that cholesterol levels in the cells regulate IL1b production by the Lpin2 deficient immune cells. To investigate the cholesterol synthesis in the bone marrow cells from cmo and Lpin2 deficient mice, expression of genes involved in cholesterol biosynthesis was performed using quantitative PCR method. We found that the expression of several cholesterol biosynthesis pathway genes is attenuated in cmo mice-derived cells, suggesting that difference in the levels of cholesterol in the cells might be involved in the susceptibility/resistance from the cmo disease.

title: Qualitative Phytochemical Analysis of a Tropical Plant in Search for a Cancer Treatment
abstract: According to the CDC approximately 38.4% of men and women will be diagnosed with cancer at some point during their lifetimes (based on 2013–2015 data). My own aunt lost her second battle with cancer a little over two years ago, her devotion to Moringa Oleifera is the inspiration for this project. In Ethno-Medicine arena, Moringa Oleifera is known as the "miracle" tree. The overall goal of this research project is to extract cancer fighting (antioxidant) properties (if any).The preliminary results after phase I of this project reveal the presence of saponin and glycosides/glycolipids in some of the samples tested. Saponin is just one of the important naturally occurring antioxidants thought to be in Moringa. Saponins are considered to have strong antitumor effect on many cancer cells. “Several saponins inhibit tumor cell growth by cell cycle arrest and apoptosis with IC50 values up to 0.2 mM...found beneficial targeted on inhibition of tumor angiogenesis by suppressing its inducer in the endothelial cells of blood vessels, and then on prevention of adhering, invasion, and metastasis of tumor cells,” (Man, 2010). Further experiments are needed to analyze the rest of the samples and identify the most promising anti-cancerous properties. Once the anti-cancerous properties are identified, conduct In-Vivo and In-Vitro anti—cancer assays.

title: Grape Ripening inside and Outside the Fruit Region
abstract: Grape growth and wine production are dependent on location, temperature, and time. The time required for grapes to ripen also varies by species of grape and location of the grape cluster on the vine. There are two main regions on a grape vine, the fruit region (FR), and outside the fruit region (OFR). The FR is the lower-middle area of the vine where the majority of the fruit grows. The region OFR consists of the upper part of the vine where there is less fruit and more foliage. Throughout many harvest periods, Fero Vineyards & Winery has determined that grapes in the OFR ripen at a slower rate than the fruit in the FR. This is due to the amount of direct sunlight and leaf exposure. FR grapes receive a moderate to high amount of direct sunlight because the leaves are pruned in this area and are not covering the fruit. The OFR grapes receive less direct sunlight because they are covered by leaves. Direct sunlight has photosynthetic effects on ripening rates of grapes through its effects on the vine’s leaves. This is because leaves provide the grapes with sugar to make them sweeter. Thus grapes outside of the fruit region do not receive the benefits of sunlight which affects their rate of ripening. Wine production proceeds almost exclusively from FR grapes, presenting an opportunity to reduce waste and increase production by determining when OFR grapes can be harvested. While general characteristics of wine grape behavior is well known, regional variations in climate and sunlight require any model of grape ripening to be based primarily on local data. This research project focuses on the time dependence of ripeness for Pinot Noir, Lemberger, Riesling, and Gruner Veltliner grapes both FR and OFR. Ripeness is determined by the balance of brix (sugar content), ph, and titratable acidity. This data will aid Fero Vineyards & Winery in harvest time estimates and possible economic benefits from creating new OFR-based products. Sources: Zoecklein, B W, and B H Gump. title: Sublimation Process of Ibuprofeniconamide Eutectic
abstract: Drug eutectic can effectively improve drug activity and bioavailability, especially for the clinical effect of oral drugs with poor water solubility.Ibuprofen is a kind of antipyretic, analgesic drug, but its water solubility is poor, its clinical effect is not good. Ibuprofen-nicotinamide eutectic was successfully prepared by sublimation crystallization technique, which solved the problem of poor water solubility of ibuprofen and achieved good clinical effect. In this paper, the experimental temperature of ibuprofen-nicotine eutectic prepared by sublimation crystallization technique is 85℃, the experimental temperature of ibuprofen placed in low temperature region is 75℃, and the total pressure is a standard atmospheric pressure. The mass flow rate of carrier gas is 30 ml/min. And it has high yield and purity. It is proved again that sublimation crystallization technology has great scientific research and commercial value.

title: Sustained Delivery of Phenotypic Regulators of T-Cells
abstract: T-cells are the critical helper, effector and regulatory cells of the adaptive immunity and are essential for life. However, defects in their number and function can contribute to tissue and organ specific inflammatory autoimmune diseases (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, etc.). A shared feature of T-cell mediated autoimmune disorders is an upregulation of pro-inflammatory T-cell subsets, often accompanied by a deficiency in the number of regulatory T-cells (T regs ). T regs lose their capacity to modulate the function of other immune cells and adopt a pro-inflammatory phenotype, secreting pro-inflammatory cytokines. This process is mediated, in part, through the IL-6/IL-6R axis in a pro-inflammatory microenvironment. We hypothesize that the local metabolic regulation of T-cells in affected tissues can restore their numbers and function, thereby mitigating the symptoms and underlying cause of inflammation. To test the hypothesis, we use small molecule immunomodulators (SMIs) of T-cells that have been previously shown to modulate T-cell phenotype in vitro. However, their small size and hydrophobicity precludes efficient delivery and therefore require high doses which contributes to undesired systemic side effects in vivo. To enhance the efficacy of SMIs, we designed a biomaterial-based system to sustain the local delivery of SMIs and suppress autoreactive T-cells and improve T reg function. We developed a polymer hydrogel to retain and release the bioactive SMIs by directly conjugating the SMIs to a biopolymer via an ester linkage in a crosslinked hydrogel. We used spectrophotometry to quantify SMI loading onto the scaffold and cell counting and flow cytometry to determine any expansion and phenotypic changes. We characterized the conjugate using spectrophotometry (λ = 360 nm) and quantified a ~5% degree of substitution of SMI. Furthermore, the SMI-polymer conjugate reduced IL-17 + T-cells by ~15% and expanded IL-10 + T-cells by ~2 fold compared to the controls without any SMI stimulation. The reduction in IL-17 + T-cells was directly proportional to the reduction in IL-6 receptor expression on T-cells. In summary, the SMI-polymer conjugate modulated the activity of autoreactive T-cells and improved T reg function, supporting its utility as a phenotypic regulator of T-cells.

title: Extraction of Dicarboxylic Acids from Fermentation Broth and Analysis By HPLC
abstract: Long dicarboxylic acids (DCAs), are used in the production of polymers, polyesters, and personal care products. However, the chemical process to make these compounds is unfavorable due the petroleum-based feedstock necessary to start the reactions. One alternative, renewable, and efficient method for the production of DCAs is through biotechnology. This study focused on improving methods for extraction and analysis of C18 DCAs in fermentation broth. We tested alternative methods of optimizing extraction conditions in order to reduce costs because pure C18:0 and C18:1 DCAs can sell for approximately 122 $/g. Solubility tests were performed on C18 DCA, C12 DCA, and stearic acid and it was determined that C12 DCA may be an adequate substitute for C18 DCA in testing; however using C12 DCA required changes to the analytical method in order to resolve peaks. The optimized method for analyzing C12 DCA used a decreased flow rate and an increased column oven temperature. The mobile phase was changed from an isocratic mixture of methanol, water, and acetic acid (v/v, 90:9.9:0.1) to a gradient between water with 0.1% (v/v) formic acid and acetonitrile with 0.1% (v/v) formic acid. Finally, an extraction method was developed for C12 DCA that had an average recovery yield of 92.9%. By optimizing the extraction process with C12 DCA, we obtained useful information for the process of optimizing extraction of C18 from fermentation broth.

title: AKT but Not MYC Promotes Reactive Oxygen Species-Mediated Cell Death in Oxidative Culture
abstract: Oncogenes can generate metabolic vulnerabilities in cancer cells. Here, we tested how AKT and MYC affect the ability of cells to shift between respiration and glycolysis. Using immortalized mammary epithelial cells, we discovered that constitutively active AKT but not MYC induced cell death in galactose culture, where cells must rely on oxidative phosphorylation for energy generation. However, the negative effects of AKT were short-lived, and AKT-expressing cells recommenced growth after ~15 days in galactose. To identify the mechanisms regulating AKT-mediated cell death, we used metabolomics and found that AKT cells dying in galactose upregulated glutathione metabolism. Next, using proteomics, we discovered that AKT-expressing cells dying in galactose upregulated nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, a marker of sensitivity to oxidative stress. We measured levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and discovered that galactose induced ROS in cells expressing AKT but not MYC. Additionally, ROS were required for the galactose-induced death of AKT-expressing cells. We then tested whether these findings could be replicated in breast cancer cell lines with constitutively active AKT signaling. Indeed, we found that galactose induced rapid cell death in breast cancer cell lines and that ROS were required for galactose-induced cell death. Our collective results demonstrate that AKT but not MYC induces a metabolic vulnerability in cancer cells, namely the restricted flexibility to use oxidative phosphorylation.

title: Design & Development of 3D Printed Polymeric Structure for Pharmaceutical(s) Delivery
abstract: 3D printing as an advanced manufacturing process provides a unique opportunity to design and develop complex structure as opposed to using traditional manufacturing techniques. 3D printing encompasses the benefits: agile and robust manufacturing, reduce the cost, reduction in turnaround times, and reliability. 3D printing of pharmaceuticals is especially advantageous for personalized medicine, making multi-drug pills where current manufacturing processes unable to do that. Traditional pharmaceutical processes and tools for the manufacturing of pills have changed relatively little for over a century. Traditional pharmaceutical manufacturing focus on large-scale batches and little flexibility in the manufacturing process due to the multi-step process. Current direct compression manufacturing process unable to make multi-drug pills due to challenges of multiple active material processing, limitation on compression, and pill size control. As an advanced manufacturing technique, 3D printing has the potential to develop personalized medicine, multi-drug pills. It is an exciting branch of research and it requires research and development to utilize the full potential. The research goal for this work is the design and development of a 3D printed polymeric structure for pharmaceutical(s) delivery. There are several 3D printing processes available and we will focus on pressure-assisted microsyringe (PAM) printing. PAM is well suited for the pharmaceutical industry due to its capability of handling materials at low temperature. Specific research objectives will be (i) develop a methodology for manufacturing 3D printed structure suitable for pharmaceutical(s) delivery, (ii) study the process parameters (nozzle size, printing pressure) that will affect the printed structure. The research outcome is expected to contribute to 3D printing fundamentals and develop personalized medicine.

title: Modeling the Controlled Release of Risperidone from PLGA Microsphere Formulations
abstract: My research is focused on how to improve the predictions of the in vivo effects of controlled release of the specific drug, risperidone. Risperidone is used to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and autistic irritability. To accomplish our goal, we are using an existing mathematical model that simulates how a general drug leaves a poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) polymer (PLGA) microsphere in vitro. We are adapting the model considering the characteristics of risperidone. So far, we have taken existing in vitro data from literature and digitized it. From there we considered the first phase of in vitro release after an initial burst to be a diffusion-controlled release regime described by Fickian diffusion with a constant diffusion coefficient. We used parameter estimation to fit the Risperidone initial burst amount and diffusion coefficients through different formulations of microspheres. Now we are looking into what happens, particularly to the second release regime of pore degradation-controlled release, when certain properties are changed, such as particle size, molecular weight, and the PLA/PGA ratios. Later we will adapt the in vitro model to an in vivo one using mass transport and pharmacokinetics of risperidone released from PLGA to create a prediction for how risperidone is delivered in the body. We will validate the final in vivo model with existing data. This approach can be compared with proposed in vitro-in vivo correlations in the literature.

title: A Systems Biology Model of Myeloid-Derived Suppressor Cells and Cancer Immunotherapy
abstract: Some malignant diseases can cause major changes to the immune system, which prevents the body from properly protecting itself from threats. Immuno-suppressive diseases like cancer, HIV, and AIDS disable the body’s ability to fight against pathogens. This begs the question that there must be a procedure to restore the body’s immune system, so it can function properly. This is why myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are extremely valuable to the immune system. These cells can serve many functions because they change into different types of cells depending on the situation at hand. When the immune system is activated, an MDSC can change into macrophages or dendritic cells, but when the immune system is not activated, it stays as a MDSC. Macrophages and dendritic cells are white blood cells that can sense a pathogen in the body, alert the immune system, and destroy it. Tumor Associated Macrophages or TAMs are the type of macrophages MDSCs morph into when they do differentiate. TAMs have been shown to have the potential of interacting negatively with the tumor cells by attacking it. The methodology of this research will use mathematical modeling of differential equations using MATLAB software to model the dynamics of MDSC and TAMs and their interactions with tumors. Mathematical modeling gives the flexibility of testing many different stimuli easily (quickly and cheaply) and mechanistically. I have combined two existing models and data from the literature. The first model considers MDSCs in the tumor microenvironment without any treatment and with a treatment. This model tests how each change affects the MDSC response. The second model shows how TAMs can be activated into two phenotypes to attack or ignore tumors. Validation of the combined MATLAB model will be done by comparing to data from collaborators and from published experimental studies.

title: Effect of Feed Flow Rate and Precipitate Concentration on the Precipitation Process for the Purification of Monoclonal Antibody
abstract: Precipitation can be a highly effective step in the initial capture of monoclonal antibodies (mAb). High yield of the precipitates can be produced continuously in a tubular reactor with cross-linking and volume exclusion agents. The integration with tangential flow microfiltration for the dewatering and wash stages would allow for high removal of impurities creating a feasible fully continuous precipitation process for the purification of mAbs. However, current issues with this process are the low impurity removal rates and low yield of the final product. The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of feed flow rate and the precipitate concentration on increasing the critical flux and product yield. The higher the critical flux, the higher the permeate flux, which would enable the membranes to remove more impurities. In our experiments, human serum Immunoglobulin G (IgG) was used as a model protein. The IgG precipitates (99.8% yield) were produced through a tubular reactor using zinc chloride and polyethylene glycol as the cross-linking and volume exclusion agent, respectively. The solutions were mixed with static mixers with a residence time of 30 seconds. Critical flux experiments were performed with a total recycle system, with the inlet feed flow rate varied to examine its effect on the critical flux. Re-dissolution experiments were performed using different IgG precipitate concentrations and buffer conditions to improve the overall product yield. Results have shown that a decrease in feed flow rate can increase the critical flux, and forming precipitates using a higher protein titer can prevent product re-dissolution and increase yield. These results provide important insights for the improved design of a precipitation – microfiltration process for initial capture/purification of a monoclonal antibody product.

title: Salt Loading Effects in Cathepsin B KO Mice on Renal Enac and Blood Pressure
abstract: Cathepsin B is among a myriad of proteases that cleaves and activates the renal epithelial sodium channel (ENaC). ENaC expressed in the distal tubule and collecting duct cells of the kidney play a key role in sodium balance and blood pressure regulation. Salt loading results in the development of hypertension in the salt sensitive kidney. We investigated the mechanism by which salt loading regulates the activity of Cathepsin B and ENaC in the kidney. We hypothesized that Cathepsin B knock out mice develop hypertension after salt loading, but the effect is attenuated when compared to wild type mice. We examined ENaC subunit protein expression in kidney cortex lysates and native tissues by Western blotting and immunohistochemistry, respectively. We performed activity assays for cathepsin B and other proteases that cleave and activate ENaC including furin and kallikrein. We measured urinary sodium and potassium levels using a SmartLyte analyzer to correlate changes in blood pressure in these mice. Taken together, our data suggest cathepsin B plays an essential role in regulating ENaC activity and blood pressure, but other proteases contribute to this regulation.

title: Quantifying Mass Changes at a Peg Surface Complexed with Alpha-Cyclodextrin
abstract: αCyclodextrin is a unique molecule because of its hydrophobic interior cavity and hydrophilic exterior. This interior cavity can create inclusion complexes with a variety of hydrophobic guest molecules, including resveratrol, a hydrophobic molecule naturally found in red wine and grapes. This system has been well quantified using Electron Impedance Spectroscopy, Cyclic Voltammetry, and X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy, but not yet with electrochemical Quartz Crystal Microbalance (eQCM). eQCM provides insight into the surface coverage of the system. It quantifies the bonds between the Poly(ethyl-glycol) and αCyclodextrin by measuring the changes in mass, as a function of frequency change. Understanding this system has implications for the field of biosensors, point-of-care tools, and any sensor that could benefit from the sensing of a guest molecule with properties similar to Resveratrol. The use of eQCM allows for mass measurements of the αCyclodextrin-PEG system. Understanding the mass changes in such a system allows for analysis of reusability and reproducibility in the context of reusable sensors. Within a flow cell, eQCM, setup, αCyclodextrin-PEG system was modified onto a gold electrode using thiol-poly(ethyl-glycol) carboxyl-terminated (PEG-CT). A decrease in frequency (proportional to an increase in mass) would be seen upon PEG-CT attachment. After this modification, αCD was introduced to the system and attached to the PEG-CT molecules further decreasing the frequency (increasing the mass).Upon introduction of Resveratrol to the system, Resveratrol and αCD create an inclusion complex, removing the αCD from the surface, which would display a decrease in mass and increase in frequency.

title: Production of Dicarboxylic Acids By Biotransformation of Oleic Acid Using Candida Viswanathii
abstract: Dicarboxylic acids (DCAs) are wildly used in biopolymer production and personal care products. Among various DCAs, long-chain dicarboxylic acids (LCDCAs) are used mostly in production of biodegradable polyesters and polyamides such as nylon. Production of DCA through biotransformation has drawn great interest from researchers recently for sustainability reasons. Previous studies have demonstrated that the yeast Candida viswanathii can potentially be used for production of dicarboxylic acids from a variety of different fatty acids, some of which are found in distillers corn oil (DCO), a byproduct of dry grind ethanol production. In this work, small scale fermentations of Candida viswanathii under various controlled conditions were conducted. As one of the major components in DCO, oleic acid was chosen as a model feedstock. Conversions with both the free acid and the methyl ester were explored. Products extracted from fermentation broth were analyzed with a previously developed high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) method. Initial results indicate the consumption rate of oleic acid was faster than that of methyl oleate. Among components extracted from fermentation broth, DCAs were detected at lower levels than expected based on feedstock consumption. Improvements to the extraction protocol are being explored to ensure high recovery of DCA. In addition, interfering medium components imposed difficulty in quantifying concentrations of DCA with the existing HPLC method. Adjustment of column temperature in the HPLC method reduced such signal interference.

title: Testing Methyltransferase Inhibitors to Therapeutically Target Glioblastoma Cancer Cells
abstract: Glioblastoma is an extremely aggressive and deadly cancer where patients have limited therapeutic treatment options. Currently, most patients must resort to chemotherapy or surgery in order to treat glioblastoma. Therefore, developing a viable therapeutic treatment option for patients suffering from glioblastoma would represent a major advancement. The process of protein methylation has been an understudied cellular process despite its importance, and the Graham Lab has developed novel proteomic techniques utilizing mass spectrometry to study peptide methylation. Due to the proximity of the MTAP gene (5-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase) to the tumor suppressor CDKN2A , MTAP is deleted in about 50% of glioblastomas. When MTAP is deleted, there is a buildup in the concentration of MTA (methylthioadenosine), which acts as a natural inhibitor for PRMT5, a methyltransferase enzyme responsible for cellular protein methylation, further sensitizing the cell to drug inhibition of PRMT5. Data from the Graham Lab indicates that PRMT1 and PRMT5 inhibition have a synergistic effect. Furthermore, this trend should only selectively target glioblastoma cells that have MTAP deleted, as normal cells with MTAP should be able to withstand drug-mediated inhibition. We hypothesize that when both PRMT1 and PRMT5 are inhibited within a cancer cell deleted for MTAP , the cell will die because its methyltransferase enzymes will no longer be able to methylate essential proteins. To test this hypothesis, we will culture MTAP -deleted cancer cell lines engineered to overexpress either luciferase (negative control) or MTAP (reconstitution of MTAP). We will treat the cells with different concentrations of PRMT1 and PRMT5 drug inhibitors and analyze cell growth. We will then lyse the cells and use both High pH SCX (Strong Cation Exchange) and Sequential IAP (Immunoaffinity Purification) to enrich for methylated peptides and investigate the samples using mass spectrometry. Both SCX and IAP are powerful proteomic enrichment techniques that can be used to study methylated forms of arginine. Using the mass spectrometry results, we will identify differential methylation sites to determine the impact of global arginine methylation. We expect to pinpoint a specific concentration of PRMT1/PRMT5 inhibitors that will selectively target cells deleted for MTAP while keeping normal cells alive. We expect for the PRMT1 and PRMT5 inhibitors to display a synergistic effect. Additionally, we expect to learn more about how methyltransferase inhibitors impacts cellular survival. What we learn about protein methylation has the potential to advance our knowledge on cellular processes, and similar methods can be applied to therapeutically target different diseases.

title: Effects of Altered Quorum Sensing Regulatory Networks on Pseudomonas Aeruginosa pathogenesis
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic bacterial pathogen that commonly causes chronic lung infections in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients. People with CF acquire P. aeruginosa from their environment, after which the pathogen undergoes genetic and phenotypic changes to adapt to the lung. Many of the adaptations occur in quorum sensing (QS) systems, which regulate cell-to-cell communication that aids in coordination of group behaviors within a bacterial population. P. aeruginosa expresses a wide variety of QS-regulated phenotypes that can be used as prognostic markers of infectious stage within each patient. This study examines the link between the accumulation of QS genetic mutations and phenotypic expression in P. aeruginosa laboratory strains and clinical isolates. We utilized several plate-based and colorimetric assays to quantify the production of pyocyanin, rhamnolipids, and protease from the lab strain PA14, its QS gene deletion standards, and paired clinical early- and late-stage chronic infection isolates across 16 patients. Exoproduct production of each isolate was compared to the mean production of pooled isolates to classify high producing (QS-sufficient) and low producing (QS-deficient) isolates. We also sequenced important QS genes in these clinical isolates to identify mutations in order to link changes between genotype and phenotype. Future research of the QS regulatory networks will identify whether reversion of genotype will result in corresponding phenotypic changes in QS-deficient chronic infection isolates.

title: Assessing Gut Transport of Methionine and Lysine in Fast-Growing Rainbow Trout
abstract: Commercial aquaculture is growing at a rate of 7% per year and uses marine-derived fish meal to feed finfish and shellfish worldwide. However, fish meal supplies are limited and the future growth of aquaculture depends on the discovery of alternative sources of protein to feed fish. One promising alternative is plant-derived fish meal, however plant proteins lack sufficient levels of methionine and lysine for fish dietary requirements. A genetically selected line of rainbow trout that grows more rapidly on a plant protein diet was compared to a non-selected line. It was hypothesized that genetically selected rainbow trout uptake lysine and methionine more efficiently in their gut via more numerous amino acid transporters as compared to non-selected fish. Amino acid uptake and total amino acids were assessed in plasma over time using [C13] and [N15] isotopically labeled methionine and lysine measured by LCMS. Amino acid transporter expression in the gut was assessed using qPCR. Results show amino acid uptake in rainbow trout selected for rapid growth on a plant-protein diet is greater than the uptake observed in non-selected fish. Quantitative PCR of amino acid transporters in the proximal intestine also show various levels of expression over time consistent with levels of amino acid uptake.

title: Aggregation of Gold Nanoparticles and Virus Complexes with Osmolytes
abstract: Detection of viruses is difficult because they are some of the smallest microorganisms in the world. Typical virus detection techniques utilize expensive reagents and require highly-trained personnel. One alternative method to detecting viruses is through use of citrate capped gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) and osmolytes. When in the presence of osmolytes, viruses and AuNP complexes will aggregate due to hydrophobic interactions, increasing the hydrodynamic diameter of the AuNPs. Size changes can be detected using methods of dynamic light scattering (DLS) and a red shift in ultra violet visual spectroscopy (UV-Vis). The research conducted consists of multiple trials using 15 nm AuNPs to detect the behavior of aggregation with two model viruses. AuNPs were synthesized by reducing gold (III) chloride trihydrate using trisodium citrate. The size of the synthesized AuNP was confirmed using dynamic light scattering (DLS), which measures size and UV-Vis absorbance, which measures the absorbance of light. Next, the virus was purified via dialysis with 1000 kDa dialysis tubing in 4.3 mM pH 7.2 phosphate buffer (PB) and size exclusion chromatography. Once purified, a 1:10 dilution was performed to obtain 5 different concentrations of virus. Additionally, 1 nM and 1 μM bovine serum albumin (BSA) and 4.3 mM PB alone were used as controls to show that only virus-AuNPs complexes were aggregated by osmolytes. AuNPs were coated by rotating for 20 hours. Once coated, a benchmark measurement was taken before aggregation with osmolytes and salt. To aggregate, the coated samples were spun down, the supernatant was removed and the samples were resuspended in 1 mL of 1 M glycine, mannitol, or sodium chloride. Finally, the aggregated samples were measured using UV-Vis and DLS. Two viruses were used to test the ability of AuNPs to detect virus. It was hypothesized that a 1:1 ratio of AuNP diameter to virus diameter would provide the best results because it would be easier for similarly sized particles to interact with each other’s geometries. Different concentrations of porcine parvovirus (PPV), diameter 18-26 nm, with 15 nm AuNP complexes showed conclusive aggregation when 1 M mannitol was added. Bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV), diameter 40-60 nm, and 15 nm AuNP complexes showed concentration dependent aggregation with 1 M mannitol as well. The data provides evidence that the use of osmolytes to induce aggregation of AuNP and virus complexes shows promise as a simple, inexpensive virus detection method.

title: Treatment of Low Back Pain Using an Injectable Tissue Specific Scaffold
abstract: Low back pain (LBP) will affect 70-80% of the global population at some point during their lifetime. The main cause of LBP is known to be intervertebral disc degeneration, that causes spinal nerve impingement, leading to pain that may radiate throughout the body. Current treatment methods include prescription medications and invasive spinal fusion surgery which have many drawbacks and do not target the root of the problem. Therefore, this project involved using decellularized intervertebral disc tissue from pig as a scaffold to restore disc height and rejuvenate local cells to minimize LBP. This objective was accomplished through a thermally gelling collagen hydrogel, allowing for minimally invasive delivery to the core of the disc. Hydrogels containing decellularized tissue and greater than 2 mg/ml collagen formed macroscopically intact gels and thermal gelation kinetics results revealed that increasing collagen concentration led to a firmer and more viscous gel. Gelation time was also investigated to allow for optimal injectable delivery of the gel. Overall, intact gels were successfully synthesized by combining decellularized tissue supplemented with collagen hydrogels. Further work aims at improving the robustness of the gels.

title: Comparison of Mathematical Solution Approaches for a Simple Theoretical Dialysis Model
abstract: Emerging new disciplines and technologies have made it possible to move in the direction of smaller and wearable artificial organs. This is the case of alternative treatments for renal insufficiency which may include dialysis. Miniaturization of traditional methods, such as hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis, has open the doors for the development of portable and implantable devices. On the design aspect, considerable attention is been devoted to analyze the fundamental principles governing the intended down scaling for this type of applications. Typically, the analysis involves the solution of non-trivial differential equations followed by simulation of different performance scenarios. The approach, predictive in essence, makes experimental work more effective and less intense as optimal device designing can be achieved using less resources. In this contribution, the focus is on the analysis of the mathematical methods utilized to solve the fundamental differential equations describing the dialysis phenomenon. These methods may have an impact on the prediction of performance and therefore the potential design of a device. For the typical dialysis model, two mathematical methods apply to the solution of the resulting differential equations: variable separation and the asymptotic solution. In this study, the molar species continuity equation is solved analytically using these two methods and the prediction results are compared with the numerical values. A summary of these results will be provided with important insights into the development and design of wearable artificial kidneys.

title: Estimation of Subcutaneous Electroosmotic Velocities in a 2-D Iontophoretic System: An Area Averaging Approach
abstract: Although the technique is well known since approximately 3,000 BC, transdermal drug delivery became a common practice starting only five decades ago. Initially used to treat skin disorders, today’s transdermal delivery is an alternative treatment for patients with vascular limitations, epilepsy, advance pregnancy, heart condition, artificial joints, and lumps among others. Iontophoresis, a modern version of this old technique, uses electrical field gradients over the skin to more accurately and in less time deliver drug to a specific area of the body. The process facilitates the transport of species by two mechanisms, electrophoresis and electro-osmosis. Depending on the order of magnitude of the electrical field gradient one of these two mechanisms can be dominant of the procedure. Investigating the best or most effective conditions at which electro-osmosis has an improvement impact in drug delivery is the driving force for the present effort. This is the continuation and follow up of a previous contribution presented on the topic 1 . In this contribution, the mathematical governing expressions capturing the fluid dynamic of the system, coupled with the electrical field, is solved by applying the method of spatial averaging to the bulk movement of the transporting fluid. In addition, explicit analytical expressions are derived for the local and average electrostatic potential, and the local and average electroosmotic velocity. Illustrations of how a 2D electrical field can aid in increasing drug delivery with the target system. Practical conclusions and potential applications with less disruptive treatment protocol are discussed. title: Improved Specificity and Sensitivity of CRISPR/Cas12a Using Toehold Modified Crrnas
abstract: Improved specificity and sensitivity of CRISPR/Cas12a using toehold modified crRNAs The CRISPR/Cas (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats/CRISPR-associated) systems, including the most popular CRISPR/Cas9 system, have been used primarily for genome editing applications. CRISPR accomplishes this by utilizing both a Cas protein which acts as molecular scissors as well as a guide RNA which dictates the protein where to cut. Through simple swapping of the guide RNA, different 19-23 base sequences can be targeted for editing. Additionally, a different CRISPR/Cas system based on Cas12a, also known as Cpf1, has been used for both genome editing as well as nucleic acid detection. Cas12a has been recently used for nucleic acid detection by utilizing its single turn-over cleavage of target DNA (cis cleavage) along with a multiple turnover, collateral cleavage of non-specific single stranded DNA (trans cleavage). To quantify the amount of DNA, CRISPR/Cas12a has been combined with Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) based nucleic acid reporters in two different studies named as DNA endonuclease-targeted CRISPR trans reporter (DETECTR) and specific high-sensitivity enzymatic reporter unlocking (SHERLOCK) 1-3 . Both methods rely on recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) to amplify the target DNA to achieve the required sensitivity necessary for nucleic acid detection. Furthermore, they are somewhat non-specific. To address these issues, we proposed making modifications to the 3’ end of the crRNA (CRISPR RNA) that could improve the specificity and sensitivity of the DETECTR or SHERLOCK assay. The method we utilized is the addition of nucleic acids on the 3’ end of the crRNA forming a toehold loop. We hypothesize that by adjusting the length of toehold sequences, the ratio of trans- to cis- cleavage can be significantly altered allowing for an increase in sensitivity and specificity. By adjusting the ratio of trans- to cis- cleavage the toehold loop can be used for either detection (by increasing trans- to cis- cleavage ratio) or specific cutting (by decreasing trans- to cis- cleavage ratio). This will have huge implications for both disease detection and in vivo gene editing utilizing the CRISPR/Cas12a system. Chen JS, Ma E, Harrington LB, et al. title: In Vivo Remediation of Contaminants in the GI Tract
abstract: As a result of industrialization and urbanization, persistent organic pollutants can be found anywhere from soil to water to biological systems. High levels of contaminants in the body, like polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), are associated with various health risks such as hypertension, high blood pressure, and metabolic disruption. To reduce the body burden, polymeric nanocomposites were synthesized from functional monomers, including styrene, vinyl pyridine, etc. and novel crosslinkers, including quercetin multiacrylate (QMA). It was hypothesized that their aromatic properties would allow these polymers to have a high affinity for PCBs. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) confirmed the presence of the components of the polymer, while wash analysis ensured a high conversation and incorporation of QMA in environments that resembled that of the gastrointestinal tract. The affinity of the polymer to the contaminant was shown in the kinetic and binding studies, which demonstrated that after 24 hours, an average of 92% of PCB-1 in solution was bound to the polymer. With further development, it is expected that these polymers will ultimately be applied to remediate the GI tract of the burden of these contaminants by preventing their absorption and aiding their expulsion.

title: Elucidation of the Ochratoxin A Biosynthetic Pathway via Heterologous Expression in Aspergillus nidulans
abstract: Ochratoxin A (OTA) is a secondary metabolite produced by the Penicillium and Aspergillus fungi genera. OTA is a food toxin that has been shown in previous studies to be carcinogenic, immunotoxic, and genotoxic, and has been found to be produced under shipping conditions in cereals and fruits. Consensus biosynthetic pathways have been found in Aspergillus carbonarius , but biosynthetic pathways in other species have not been verified. The current biosynthetic pathway utilizes polyketide synthase (PKS), non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS), Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases and halogenase enzymes to synthesize OTA. We first verify the biosynthetic pathway of OTA via heterologous expression in Aspergillus nidulans . Our experiments yield the OTA intermediates 7-carboxymellein and 7-methylmellein via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS), indicating that the proposed biosynthetic pathway failed to yield ochratoxin B at the peptide sythetase step. The absence of phenylalanine ethyl ester indicates either the failure of phenylalanine to esterify properly or the absence of non-ribosomal peptide synthetase for lack of transcription factors to activate the gene encoding NRPS. Transcription factors were found in Aspergillus carbonarius and OTA was heterologously expressed again in Aspergillus nidulans. Future directions include investigation of the possibility of hybrid PKS-NRPS genes in OTA production. Furthermore, characterization of the domains of PKS and NRPS can elucidate the mechanisms by which the 7-methylmellein and ochratoxin B is formed, respectively. Upon elucidation of these mechanisms, possibilities of gene regulation via gene therapy or similar approaches can be used to mediate OTA production in food production and transport.

title: Characterizing a Novel Brain-Targeted Polymeric Nanoparticle Platform
abstract: Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder that leads to significant brain damage. Currently approved therapeutics treat symptoms, but do not slow down the progression of disease. There are several drugs that can slow progression, but delivery is challenging due to the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Polyanhydride nanoparticles (NPs) can improve therapeutic efficacy for brain delivery by crossing the BBB and releasing the drug at the right time. The goal of this project is to develop and characterize targeted NP-based drug delivery methods that will slow down the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, such as PD. There are multiple hurdles to delivering therapeutics to the brain. They need to cross the BBB, target the diseased area of the brain, and often deliver payloads to specific organelles or pathological features associated with cells in this area. Using a novel targeted functionalization polyanhydride NP platform, each of these hurdles can be addressed effectively and in a cascading manner. In order to optimize therapeutic efficacy, however, NP-drug interaction properties need to be well characterized. By better understanding drug-NP interactions, the NP synthesis conditions can be precisely tuned so that the therapeutics can be released at the right time, with the correct dose needed to slow disease progression. In this study, the interaction of NPs functionalized with a cationic ligand, triphenylphosphonium, known to have BBB-targeting capabilities, with several anti-neurodegenerative drugs was characterized and compared to the same formulations without functionalization. A correlation with drug hydrophobicity was found regardless of functionalization, where more sustained release was observed for hydrophobic drugs over multiple days, while hydrophilic drugs experienced a large “burst” release within the first day with trace amounts released thereafter. However, the difference in encapsulation efficiency (EE) between hydrophilic and hydrophobic drugs was not significant. Using the surfactant span-80 during NP synthesis, however, raised the EE of hydrophobic drugs in non-functionalized NPs but had no apparent effect on functionalized NPs, nor on the overall release kinetics for either formulation, regardless of the encapsulated drug. Lastly, the use of surfactant lowered the EE of hydrophobic drugs in functionalized NPs but had no apparent effect on non-functionalized NPs, nor on the overall release kinetics for either formulation. Ongoing and future studies are focusing more deeply on drug-NP interaction properties, surface charge, and cellular internalization efficiency using neurons, microglia, astrocytes and endothelial cells.

title: Development of RNAi Tools for Gene Knockdown in Rhodosporidium Toruloides
abstract: Development of RNAi Tools for Gene Knockdown in Rhodosporidium toruloides August Finke 1 , Anne M. Ruffing 1 , James Kirby 2 , and John M. Gladden 2 Bioenergy and Defense Technologies, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM Biomass Science and Conversion Technologies, Sandia National Laboratories, Emeryville, CA Rhodosporidium toruloides is a yeast used to produce biofuels due to its fast growth, high lipid production, and ability to use different carbon sources for growth. Experiments were performed to develop and test RNA interference (RNAi) tools that can later be used to increase biofuel potential in R. toruloides . RNAi is a biological process that suppresses or knockdowns genes. In this study, a green fluorescent protein (GFP) – bisabolene synthase fusion gene, was randomly integrated into R. toruloides . GFP served to measure gene expression. An RNAi construct designed to produce double stranded RNA that knocks down GFP and bisabolene production was randomly integrated into the strain containing the GFP-bisabolene synthase fusion protein. GFP was measured using flow cytometry; optical density measurements were taken to track growth; and bisabolene production was quantified through the collection of dodecane layers and analysis by gas chromatography. The bisabolene and GFP knockdown exhibited a positive correlation, showing that the RNAi successfully knocked down the whole mRNA that coded for the GFP-bisabolene fusion gene. This RNAi technique can be applied to knockdown genes that would improve biofuel production in R. toruloides . title: Determining Pharmaceutical Powder Wettability
abstract: In this work different methodologies that are used to measure the wettability of powders are studied in detail. It has been recognized that the different manufacturing process would significantly change the wetting behavior of material. In addition, the wetting properties of raw and intermediate material directly affect the dissolution performance and bioavailability. For this reason, the characterization of wetting properties is inevitable for quality control in advanced pharmaceutical manufacturing. Several techniques have been developed to identify wettability of powders. These include the sessile droplet, capillary rise, immersion and condensation methods. The sessile drop method (i.e. drop penetration method) is the most common method. In this method a single liquid droplet is released to a powder bed and the contact angle of the liquid is then measured on the powder bed. This method is the easiest to replicate, but it is also very sensitive to powder bed condition. For instance, air may get trapped inside the powder bed. The capillary rise method is a layer of powder and the fluid is pushed up through it. In the immersion method the powder bed is placed under the liquid and the phase interaction between the solid and liquid is observed. In the condensation method the resting drops on the surface are analyzed. Another frequently used technique is the capillary rise method. Here, the powder will be packed into a tube and the test fluid can interact with the powder by moving up the tube. Sources of error in this method are the possible movement of the tube during testing as well as the inability that occurs due to use of non-Newtonian liquids or liquids with contact angles over 90°. The immersion method involves taking the powder and submerging it into a pool of test fluid, while the condensation method involves making the test fluid into a saturated vapor and having the vapor condense into droplets on the powders surface for analysis. The immersion method can be difficult to replicate because the adhesive that is used to adhere the powder to the solid may lead to a wrong perimeter of the particle being recorded, that would lead to an incorrect conclusion. It is also likely that due to the liquid imbibition, the reported contact angle would be too small. Both immersion and condensation are harder to replicate and for that reason less commonly used when testing the wettability of a powder.

title: Determining the Effect of Zygotic Cactus on the Dorsal/Cactus Feedback Loop
abstract: Feedback loops in biology help regulate cell signaling, cell responses, and cell differentiation. The basis for differentiation lies within cell-to-cell communication through signaling. The signal of interest in this experiment is Dorsal (a NF-κB homolog). It was hypothesized that Cactus, an inhibitor of Dorsal, provides a negative feedback loop to ensure robustness of signaling during differentiation. Cactus binds to Dorsal to create a complex and prevent Dorsal from entering the nuclei to regulate target genes. The goal was to determine the role of zygotic Cactus in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster . To test whether Cactus disrupts the Dorsal gradient, embryos lacking zygotic Cactus, df(cact), were compared to the control wild type, yellow-whites. All sets of embryos contained maternal Dorsal. Embryos were collected, fixed, and stained with fluorescent antibodies. They were visualized with confocal imaging to measure fluorescence of the tagged genes. Matlab was used to analyze the images. It was found that the embryos had a high population around σ=0.15, but other populations could be present. The best fit values for β, ϒ, κ, α, and delta in the modeling equation were found to be: 0.0789, 1.7258, 1.2505, 11.7598, and 0 respectively. More data is needed to make more conclusive results.

title: Using CRISPR Cas13a to Combat the Flu Virus at the Genetic Level: A New Approach to Flu Treatment
abstract: The influenza vaccine normally provides protection from three to four strains included in the formulation. However, since the flu viruses constantly mutate, the vaccine protection decreases because it can only protect against strains included in the vaccine but not the new ones. As a result, it needs to be reformulated each year to accommodate the new strains. The vaccine is also unable to protect against pandemic strains. As a treatment approach, antiviral medications can be administered to infected patients, but often the strains are resistant to the drugs. The long-term objective of this research is to develop a new flu medication that uses CRISPR technology to target the viral genome. Highly conserved sequences in the genome are targeted by Cas13a proteins using specially designed CRISPR RNA (crRNA). Cas13a is highly selective through the use of the crRNA, which attaches to the complementary sequence in the virus genome and designates the location the Cas13a protein should cut. As a result, the flu RNA will be cut, thereby preventing viral replication, hence treating the infection. Since the crRNA targets the highly conserved regions of influenza viruses, the treatment is expected to be broadly effective against different viral strains.

title: Targeted Delivery of Parathyroid Hormones for Accelerated Fracture Repair
abstract: The goal of this project is to complete the lab-to-clinic translation of a drug that efficiently targets and promotes the rapid healing of fractured bones. The annual frequency of bone fractures in the U.S. is approximately 6.3 Million.1 Costs associated with conventional treatments and subsequent lost productivity carry a major economic burden--a problem compounded by an aging population. This increasing age demographic will continue to raise the frequency of osteoporosis and the associated rate of complicated and life-threatening fractures, with hip fractures expected to increase 160% to 500,000/year by 2040. The total estimated expenses due to hip fractures in the elderly are $20 billion/year in the U.S. alone, with half of patients unable to regain full mobility and a quarter dying within a year from associated complications. We are developing a promising solution to this problem; namely, a potent but nontoxic fracture-targeted bone anabolic agent that is injected systemically but accumulates selectively on a bone fracture surface. The targeted therapy avoids the requirement for invasive surgery and eliminates the danger of ectopic bone growth while improving the rate and quality of bone fracture repair.

title: Fundamental Analysis of Aqueous Humor Dynamics in the Human Eye
abstract: Fluid mechanics is an essential part in numerous aspects of the composition and pathology of the human eye. In particular, glaucoma, a condition caused by an increased amount of intraocular pressure, is heavily dependent on the proper flow and drainage of aqueous humor in the eye. Currently, the most popular approach to impeding the disease is through numerous types of surgeries, such as laser or incisional surgery, which reduces intraocular pressure by creating a pathway to the Schlemm’s Canal. However, minimal research has been done to improve the drugs administered to glaucoma patients nor the proficiency of the drugs being delivered to the trabecular meshwork, for example. A fundamental analysis has the potential to aid in a better comprehension of the velocity and concentration profile in the human eye to improve in the administering of drugs and validate the effectiveness of surgery on patients without damaging other functional aspects in the eye. In this contribution, the focus is on the analysis of the mathematical models used to solve fundamental differential equations describing the velocity and concentration profile in the human eye. The Navier-Stokes equation is solved using a creeping flow assumption to obtain velocity profiles within the trabecular meshwork. The resulting velocity has been coupled with the corresponding molar species continuity equation to obtain drug concentration profiles in the same local area. A summary of these findings will be provided with significant insight on improved drug treatment and the effectiveness of surgery to glaucoma patients.

title: Comparison of Keit Irmadillo™ and Mettler Toledo Reactir for Pharmaceutical Process Chemistry Reaction Monitoring
abstract: In-situ attenuated total internal reflection fourier transform mid-infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) with the ATR probe placed in the reaction vessel is a well-established technique for monitoring pharmaceutical process chemistry reactions that can reveal reaction component concentration trends, such as starting material consumption, product formation, and reaction intermediates if present. The Keit IRmadillo™ is a relatively new ATR-IR spectrometer that is being marketed as a rugged instrument for monitoring reactions in liquids and slurries and is certified for use in hazardous and potentially explosive industrial environments. The Mettler Toledo ReactIR 702L is another new ATR-FTIR instrument marketed for chemical reaction monitoring, but is a more compact unit primarily intended for use in research and development laboratories. This poster compares the IRmadillo and ReactIR 702L with the Mettler Toledo ReactIR iC10, an older ATR-FTIR instrument used extensively at GlaxoSmithKline. A major operational difference between instruments is that the ReactIR iC10 requires liquid nitrogen to cool the detector, whereas the IRmadillo and ReactIR 702L do not, which enables them to start more quickly and to run unattended indefinitely, important advantages for both lab and plant operation. However, the corresponding higher detector temperatures used by the IRmadillo and the ReactIR 702L are also expected to decrease the instrument sensitivity and increase noise, which could negatively impact reaction monitoring performance. Results from monitoring two example reactions will be presented. The first example compared all three instruments using a pharmaceutical intermediate compound manufacturing process where the slurry reaction endpoint time can vary based on certain process parameters. To compensate for this uncertainty, ATR-FTIR is used to track the reaction intermediate concentration and determine the appropriate timepoint to sample the reaction for endpoint confirmation by HPLC analysis. The second example used the well-known homogeneous solution reaction of acetic anhydride with methanol to further evaluate the IRmadillo and ReactIR iC10 instrument sensitivity, ability to detect transient reaction species, and performance with high concentration components.

title: Selective Precipitation of Haptoglobin from Human Plasma Fraction IV
abstract: Haptoglobin (Hp) is the serum protein responsible for scavenging cell-free hemoglobin (Hb), the oxygen storage and transport protein of red blood cells (RBCs). During states of hemolysis, such as extensive blood transfusion, sickle-cell anemia, or Malaria, cell-free Hb is released from RBCs into the blood stream. Cell-free Hb is toxic and can lead to tissue oxidation and hypertension. Yet, when cell-free Hb is bound to Hp, these toxic effects are inhibited, making Hp a promising therapeutic for treating states of hemolysis 1 . Unfortunately, Hp is difficult to produce and expensive. Fortunately, Hp is present within Fraction IV (F-IV), a byproduct of the Cohn process used for purification of human serum albumin 2 . However, F-IV contains various additional serum proteins and insoluble material. This study sought to determine the optimal concentration of ammonium sulfate [(NH 4­ ) 2 SO 4 ] to isolate Hp from F-IV via selective protein precipitation. Increasing amounts of (NH 4­ ) 2 SO 4 were added to 100 F-IV suspensions, creating solutions ranging from 0%─70% saturation of (NH 4­ ) 2 SO 4 . title: An Immunoglobulin G Based Steric Hindrance Assay for Protein Detection
abstract: With the imminent needs of a rapid, accurate, simple point-of-care system for global healthcare industry, electrochemical biosensors have been widely developed owing to its cost-effectiveness and simple instrumentation. However, typical electrochemical biosensors for direct analysis of proteins in human biological sample still suffer from complex biosensor fabrication, lack of general method, limited sensitivity, and matrix caused biofouling effect. To resolve these challenges, we developed a general electrochemical sensing strategy based on a steric hindrance effect on an antibody surface layer. This strategy utilizes the interaction pattern of Protein-G and immunoglobulin G (Fc and Fab regions), providing steric hindrance effect during target capturing process. The provided steric hindrance effect minimizes matrix effect caused fouling surface and altered the path of electron transfer, delivering a non-fouling and high-sensitivity detection of protein in complex matrix. Also, an enzyme based horseradish peroxidase/hydroquinone/H2O2 transduction system can also be applied to the system, demonstrating the versatility of this sensing strategy for general electrochemical sensor application. We demonstrated this platform through the detection of Tau protein and programming death ligand 1 with a sub-pico molar detection limit within 10 min, satisfying the clinical point-of-care requirements for rapid turnaround time and ultra-sensitivity.

title: Screening Powder and Binder Combinations for 3D Printing Personalized Medication
abstract: Screening Powder and Binder Combinations for 3D Printing Personalized Medication Leila Sorrells 1,2 , Shing-Yun Chang 2 , Kavin Kowsari 2 , Karthik Nagapudi 3 , Koyel Sen 2 , Bodhi sattwa Chaudhuri 2 , Anson Ma 2 1 University of South Florida; 2 University of Connecticut; 3 Genentech, Inc. Binder jetting printing is a form of 3D printing that has recently become the preferred additive method for creation of drug tablets due to its precise printing and control of drug release. It operates using inkjet print heads and a moving print bed where prints are created by repeatedly layering a powder, binding the powder with fluid, and rolling another layer of powder on top. This research focuses on using disintegration and hardness testing to determine the best combinations of powders and binders to use as a matrix for holding an active drug component for 3D printing drug tablets. Eight polymer-based binders were tested against fifteen powder mixtures created from varying concentrations of lactose monohydrate (LM), calcium sulfate hemihydrate (CSH), and sodium croscarmellose (SC). The goal was to find a combination or combinations that would reach a hardness of roughly 15 kgf and a disintegration time less than 15 minutes in 36 °C water. For all binder types, increasing CSH percentage leads to an increase in hardness. However, the binder that consistently created samples that best aligned with the hardness and disintegration goals was Kollidon, which can be introduced in the powder or in the liquid form as an aqueous solution. Samples prepared from the same percentage of Kollidon, regardless of the method of introduction, have similar properties.

title: Microfluidic Synthesis and Purification of Protein Nanoparticles
abstract: MICROFLUIDIC SYNTHESIS AND PURIFICATION OF PROTEIN NANOPARTICLES Nanoparticles have revolutionized the field of colloidal science and have been applied for a myriad of purposes in medicine, coatings, and even electronics. Many such applications, especially in medicine, necessitate precise control over parameters including size, polydispersity, and chemical content. Protein nanoparticle systems, like Abraxane®, are successful drug carriers due to their biocompatibility and biodegradability. However, nanoparticle synthesis procedures are limited in their scalability due to the critical interplay between particle size and solution conditions. Furthermore, medical applications necessitate the removal of trace chemicals and cytotoxic impurities – a challenge for nanoparticle suspensions. Here we present a scalable microfluidic process that addresses the need for high-throughput continuous production of homogenous, size-tunable, purified protein nanoparticles . Our platform takes advantage of laminar flow to enable the reproducible synthesis of monodisperse protein nanoparticles. Nanoparticle synthesis occurs via protein desolvation and controlled aggregation in the presence of ethanol, followed by cross-linking with glutaraldehyde. Laminar flow facilitates the precise control over protein, solvent, and cross-linker concentrations within the device, allowing for tuning of nanoparticle size. We validated the efficacy of our platform with the synthesis of bovine serum albumin (BSA) nanoparticles. Our results contrast with reports on the bench-scale synthesis of the ~50 nm BSA nanoparticles necessary to avoid an immun e response. Such efforts have traditionally suffered from increased polydispersity. The particles produced by our platform demonstrate superior stability and size tunability. Our system provides a 33% reduction of required solvent, and an 80% reduction of crosslinking agent compared to benchtop BSA nanoparticle synthesis. Furthermore, our platform can produce 16.2 mg/hr of crosslinked protein nanoparticles, compared with 11.3 mg/hr for benchtop synthesis. Purification is also an important challenge in nanoparticle synthesis because the removal of small molecule cytotoxic impurities typically requires time-intensive centrifugation processes. The H-filter in our platform enables purification of nanoparticles in a continuous manner by exploiting differences in diffusion times between small molecules and nanoparticles. Therefore, our platform can remove excess solvent and crosslinker, eliminating additional purification steps. The present process introduces significant improvements to current protein nanoparticle synthesis processes, potentially enabling new applications in drug delivery . The approach is general and future work includes extrapolation into a plethora of other protein and polymer-based nanoparticle systems. Additionally, the planar chip design allows for the process to be easily scaled-out for a variety of academic and industrial applications.

title: HA-CNT Nanofibers with Anti-Inflammatory Microspheres for Enhanced Nerve Regeneration
abstract: This research aims to develop a material to promote nerve growth following spinal cord injury (SCI). The proposed design is to develop a conductive nanofiber and microsphere composite for electrical stimulation induce drug delivery to improve SCI regeneration. Nanofibers were electrospun methacrylated hyaluronic acid (MeHA) with carbon nanotubes (HA-CNT). GMS were incorporated into the HA-CNT electrospinning solution. title: Implantable Air-Brushed Nonfouling Microfiber Mats for Drug Delivery
abstract: A significant challenge in the field of biomaterials is the nonspecific adsorption of proteins to implants. Upon implantation, this nonspecific protein adsorption triggers the natural foreign body response leading to encapsulation and failure of the device. Zwitterionic materials are excellent at resisting protein adsorption. For this reason, we are investigating the zwitterionic polymer poly(sulfobetaine methacrylate) (polySBMA). Our goal is to produce nonfouling polymer microfibers by air-brush spraying. We hypothesize that nonfouling air-brushed polySBMA microfiber mats will provide a breakthrough technology for implantable drug delivery vehicles. To date we have explored the influence of spraying pressure, nozzle diameter, distance to collector, polymer molecular weight, and solvent. We have also optimized the use of a photo-polymerization reaction to reduce the water solubility of the resulting microfibers, even though they are sprayed from a water based solution. To date we have demonstrated the formation of water insoluble microfibers with diameters ranging from 2.8 to 43.1 mm. On-going work includes verification of the nonfouling properties and incorporation of pseudo-drug molecules.

title: Optimization of the Chocolate Process Using Rheology.
abstract: The science behind why some chocolates are more appealing than others is based on the optimization of the entire chocolate-making/production process. This process involves cocoa nib processing, mixing, refining, tempering and molding. Proper parameters, such as conch/melanger timing, seed chocolate and temperature, will affect the final taste. Since the appeal of chocolate is based on the chocolate’s balance of viscous and elastic behavior, comparing physical properties evaluated from rheological studies can determine the optimal procedures. The Casson model is commonly used to model food dispersions and is commonly used in chocolate manufacturing. The Casson parameters, Casson yield stress and Casson plastic viscosity, define the characteristic chocolate texture and flavor. The Casson yield stress is the minimum stress required to initiate the flow and marks the transition from the solid viscoelastic stage to the liquid stage. The Casson plastic viscosity is the resistance to flow. These parameters are identified by fitting the Casson Model parameters to the steady state flow curve. Chocolate is a complex multiphase material and the transition from a solid to liquid depends on its evolving, stress dependent microstructure. In this study, more contemporary thixo-elastic-visco-plastic (TEVP) rheological models are compared to the traditional steady state Casson model. The TEVP models fit steady and transient data, with a yield stress and plastic viscosity parameters to be compared to the Casson parameters. This research highlights the tempering and refining of the United States Military Academy chocolate making process. Chocolate tempering and refining techniques are studied to determine the impact on the chocolate’s complex behavior, yielding optimal rheological parameters. First, the tempering process was analyzed by varying the seed chocolate. The viscosity of each chocolate sample was then tested using a rheometer to collect the flow curve data. Then the refining process was analyzed by varying the length of time the chocolate remained in the melanger. Again, each chocolate sample was tested using the rheometer to determine the samples’ viscosity/elasticity. Finally, the rheological parameters using the Casson model and other contemporary TEVP models were identified by fitting the models to the experimental data and then comparing to the results of a blind taste test. Models will be compared by ability to predict large amplitude oscillatory shear flow.

title: Understanding the Relationship between Citrus Fiber Suspension Rheology and the Mesoscale Arrangement of the Fibers
abstract: The pectin depleted citrus peel is a side-stream from the pectin industry that is usually discarded. An excellent way to avoid wasting this part of the fruit is to turn it into citrus fibers by means of high pressure homogenization and drying for applications in the food industry. When mixed with water, these fibers form a viscous suspension that can be used as texturizer in food products Even so, it was observed that, after dehydrating and rehydrating a citrus fiber suspension, the viscosity of the suspension decreased significantly. This study aimed to understand why the decrease in viscosity occurs by analyzing the relationship between citrus fiber structure and rheology using viscometry, and sum frequency generation (SFG) vibrational spectroscopy. The effect of acidity and basicity on the viscosity of suspensions were investigated as well, and viscosity decreased as pH decreased. SFG indicated that the mesoscale arrangement of citrus fibers changes as the viscosities change in suspensions. From the findings of this study, the packing of the particles in mesoscale changed as fibers went through the dehydration process.

title: Development of an Osteochondral Implant Using Microencapsulated Mesenchymal Stem Cells
abstract: Osteoarthritis remains a poorly treatable outcome of traumatic cartilage injury as cartilage is unable to self-repair. Transplantation of an engineered, osteochondral tissue plug has been proposed as a better way to achieve repair of cartilage defects with implants that can readily integrate with the subchondral bone. Composite materials composed of chitosan and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) have been shown to support rapid invasion and integration with host tissues post-implantation and are a promising platform for assembling such an osteochondral implant. In this study we explored the use of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) within glycosaminoglycan-chitosan capsules as a platform for generating spherical cartilage and bone tissue “modules” for use in assembling an osteochondral construct. Rat bmMSCs were suspended (1×10 7 cells/ml) in a solution of 1.5 wt% carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), 4 wt% chondroitin 4-sulfate (CS), and 1 mg/ml collagen type I. The suspension was then electrosprayed to generate uniform droplets that were captured into a stirred and grounded chitosan solution (0.6 wt%). Electrostatic interactions between negatively charged GAGs and positively charged chitosan results in the formation of hollow microcapsules (300-500 µm in diameter) entrapping MSCs at high density. The encapsulated MSCs were cultured under static conditions in either osteogenic or chondrogenic induction medium for either 28 days (osteogenic) or 42 days (chondrogenic). Between 28 and 42 days osteogenically induced capsules were maintained in MSC growth medium. Capsule cultures were sampled at intervals and analyzed to evaluate cell/biomaterial morphology, DNA content, and extracellular matrix composition. After loose capsule culture, osteogenic and chondrogenic capsules were used to generate osteochondral constructs as follows. Cultured capsules were first briefly washed with 0.1 wt% chitosan followed by a wash with 0.1 wt% glycidyl-methacrylated polygalacturonic acid (GMA-PGA) to deposit a photocrosslinkable polyelectrolyte film. A transparent cylindrical mold was then loaded with a 4 mm layer of coated osteogenic capsules followed by a 4 mm layer of coated chondrogenic capsules. The mold was then immersed in PBS and capsule fusion was induced by photocrosslinking with 400 nM light using LAP as the photoinitiator. The fused constructs were then cultured for an additional 15 days in MSC growth medium. Results to date demonstrated the feasibility of the culture, coating and photocrosslinking method of osteochondral assembly using long-term cultured GAG-chitosan capsules. In addition, GMA-PGA was found to be an efficient, photocrosslinkable surface coating for generating fused capsule constructs.
