title: Investigating Health Effects of Aerosol Particles on Single-Cells in a High-Throughput Air-Liquid Interface Platform
abstract: Air pollution and its detrimental health effects have been an increasingly alarming concern for the world. Cardiovascular diseases, chronic respiratory diseases, and different types of cancers can all be linked to air pollution effects. Furthermore, over 8.9 million people die per year from the direct effects of ambient particulate matter. One conventional method for studying the health effects of aerosol particles is to collect particulate matter (PM) from the atmosphere, resuspend the PM in cell culture media, add the PM/media to cell cultures, and assess single cell oxidative stress. However, this method does not resemble the in vivo conditions of alveolar macrophages. Alveolar macrophages are found in the alveoli of the lungs where the oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange between blood and air takes place and are a key cell type that is affected by PM. In this project, we aim to create a microfluidic air-liquid interface environment that mimics how alveolar macrophages are exposed to PM in order to study effects of PM at a single-cell level. Utilizing a microfluidic platform provides uniform microenvironment and enables high-throughput and high content single-cell analysis for hundreds of cells. We adapted a previously developed microfluidic single-cell analysis technology and developed a method for exposing cells to an air-liquid interface. We then characterized cells by microscopy and LIVE/DEAD staining to assess if cells remain viable during air exposure. Following this validation of the air-liquid interface platform, we will use it to study the single cell responses of intracellular reactive oxygen species in exposure to aerosol particles.

title: Upregulation of the Glutaminase II Pathway Contributes to Glutamate Production upon Glutaminase 1 Inhibition in Pancreatic Cancer
abstract: The targeting of glutamine metabolism specifically via pharmacological inhibition of glutaminase 1 (GLS1) has been translated into clinical trials as a novel therapy for several cancers. The results, though encouraging, show room for improvement in terms of tumor reduction. Here, we demonstrate that pancreatic tumors upregulate the production of glutamate from glutamine via the glutaminase II pathway upon GLS1 inhibition. Moreover, genetic suppression of glutamine transaminase K (GTK), a key enzyme of the glutaminase II pathway, leads to the complete inhibition of pancreatic tumorigenesis in vivo; unveiling GTK as a new metabolic target for cancer therapy. These results suggest that current trials using GLS1 inhibition as a therapeutic approach targeting glutamine metabolism in cancer should take into account the upregulation of other metabolic pathways that can lead to glutamate production; one such pathway is the glutaminase II pathway via GTK.

title: Multi-Epitopic Down-Regulating Antibodies for Cancer Immunotherapy
abstract: CD8 + effector T cells are the cytotoxic force of the immune system, and their activity is carefully regulated by signaling through their cell surface receptors. The signals delivered through these receptors can be either stimulatory or suppressive; in particular, activation of immunosuppressive proteins on the T cell surface (known as immune checkpoint receptors) dampens T cell activity and leads to exhaustion or anergy. Tumor cells have evolved to exploit this immunosuppressive pathway to evade clearance by the immune system, contributing to cancer progression. To circumvent this issue, antibody drugs have been developed against immune checkpoint proteins to competitively block their activation, allowing for efficient anti-cancer T cell activity. Although this approach has demonstrated clinical success, the majority of patients do not respond to treatment, and most responses are only partial. We aim to improve upon immune checkpoint blockade by engineering novel therapeutics that act through alternative mechanisms. To do this, we engineered bispecific antibodies that simultaneously bind to 2 non-competitive epitopes on the same immune checkpoint protein (termed multi-epitopic antibodies). This design is advantageous because in addition to blocking ligand binding, the bispecific antibody can induce cross-linking of adjacent receptors to induce receptor down-regulation. We used the yeast surface display directed evolution platform and magnetic- and fluorescence-activated cell sorting to isolate novel antibodies targeting immune checkpoint proteins, which were then used as the basis for formulating multi-epitopic antibodies. Preliminary results indicate that these engineered antibodies efficiently down-regulate immune checkpoint receptors, presenting a promising new approach for cancer immunotherapy.

title: Using Zebrafish to Identifying the Role of Wisp1 in Melanoma Metastasis
abstract: Wnt family members play an important role in many developmental processes in humans and other animals, they also have been linked to tumorigenesis. A gene named WISP1(Wnt inducting signaling pathway1), is a member of this family, it's expression is increased in melanoma(a deadly type of skin cancer) and is associated with reduced overall survival of patients diagnosed with primary melanoma. Zebrafish was the model selected for this purpose,because they have melanocytes that can become malignant and develop melanoma through specific mutations. Zebrafish also have two homologs of the gene WISP1 in their genome. Here, we knocked down each homolog of WISP1 separately in wildtype zebrafish, using MOs (Morpholino oligonucleotides) and compared their phenotype to other control groups to understand what role WISP1 plays in Zebrafish morphology and then perform a dose control experiment to ensure that the resulting phenotype is a result of the knockdown, and not any other off-target effects. title: Non-Standard Amino Acid Incorporation in Proteins for Biofilm Surface Attachment
abstract: Biofilms are consortiums of microbes in which cells stick together or on a surface embedded within a slimy extracellular matrix composed of extracellular polymeric substances mainly polysaccharides, proteins, lipids and DNA. The biofilms formed on living or non-living surfaces prevalent in hospital settings are generally by pathogenic microorganisms such as Staphylococcus spp, Escherichia coli, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa leading to numerous health infections. Microbes form biofilm in response to various factors, which include nutritional cues, or in some cases, by exposure of planktonic cells to sub- inhibitory concentrations of antibiotics. A cell switches to the biofilm mode of growth undergoes a phenotypic shift in behavior in which large suites of genes are differentially regulated and gradually develop resistance to conventional anti-microbial drugs. Therefore, in this study we are exploring the interaction of probiotic and pathogenic bacterial species to make a monolayer probiotic biofilm on any surface to prevent pathogenic biofilm attachment and formation. Usage of probiotic bacteria might lead to a possible alternative solution for inhibiting and killing pathogenic microorganisms rather than developing a new array of antibiotics.

title: Elucidating Protein Remodeling Mechanism By Molecular Chaperones
abstract: HtpG is a molecular chaperone protein found in Escherichia coli . This protein belongs to a family of ATP-dependent molecular chaperones and couples conformational changes from ATP hydrolysis to protein remodeling; HtpG assists other proteins in reaching their native conformation, preventing aggregation, and mediating targeted unfolding and disassembly. In this study mutants of HtpG defective in ATP binding or substrate binding were constructed. HtpG mutants E34A and W467R were made by site directed mutagenesis. HtpG wild type and mutant proteins were overexpressed in E. coli, collected, and purified using Fast Protein Liquid Chromatography. The purified proteins were tested for ATPase activity, stimulation of ATPase activity by substrate proteins, and prevention of aggregation assays. Both mutants studied, HtpG E34A and W467R, were defective in chaperone activity and prevention of aggregation. Comparing these mutants with their wild-type form, they exhibited decreased rates of ATP hydrolysis and were not stimulated by model substrate proteins such as rhodanese and citrate synthase. Also, in the prevention of aggregation assay using urea- denatured Rhodanese, HtpG wild-type and ATP and substrate defective mutants were unable to prevent aggregation.

title: Development of a Microfluidic Device to Study Cell-to-Cell Communication By Dynamic Sampling of Paracrine Factors
abstract: Breast cancer is the second leading cause of cancer related death in American women. Cancer cells signal to surrounding tumor stroma to produce cancer associated adipocytes, fibroblasts, and macrophages while secreted factors from stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment induce drug resistant and metastasis in cancer cells. Co-culture and conditioned media-based experiments have demonstrated that paracrine factors induce drug resistance. While multiple co-culture techniques exist, no of them are capable of dynamic sampling of extracellular media during an experiment to investigate cell-to-cell communications. To address this, a novel microfluidic device was designed, fabricated, and tested to study intercellular communications during co-culture. The device consists of three parallel channels connected by an array of 30 µm wide by 100 µm long microchannels spaced 75 µm apart to facilitate the orthogonal diffusion of biomolecules. COMSOL Multiphysics was used to model the mass transfer in the device to optimize channel length and width. The optimized device consisted of three parallel 1500 µm long with the two outermost channels for static cell culture and the center channel connected to a peristaltic pump to allow for continual perfusion and circulating of medium. The operating length of the three channels was 20 mm to allow for sufficient cell numbers for sampling of paracrine factors. Circulating media flowrates of 5, 10, and 15 µL/min were tested, with 5 µL/min providing sufficient mass transfer across the three channels with minimal shear effects on the culture cells A test device was fabricated using a combination of soft lithography and polydimethyl siloxane (PDMS) replication. The device utilized a peristaltic pump with clear, flexible tubing for constant flow of media and a three-way junction incorporating into the tubing outside of the device for dynamic sampling. Pipette-tip reservoirs were positioned at the inlets and outlets of the culture channels for media replacement. Peristaltic pump performance was characterized by running water through the tubing and timing the water collection at different pump speeds. The pipette-tip reservoirs were observed during testing to ensure media replacement without the introduction of bubbles during sampling. A careful sampling technique, which included clipping the opposite junction during sampling, was also developed to address this issue. This novel microfluidic device will be used to analyze the cell-to-cell communications between MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells, a triple negative cell line, and adipose-derived stem cells (ASCs) to study how stromal cells enhance the proliferation and drug resistance of cancer cells.

title: Synthesis and Characterization of Novel Phospholipid-Conjugated Topotecan Prodrugs for Lipid Vehicle Delivery
abstract: Current anticancer therapies face the innate challenge of proper targeting and dosing of chemotherapeutic agents. Low selectivity is a characteristic trait of many existing drugs, which results in unintended damage to healthy tissue alongside cancerous tissue that may cause dangerous short and long-term side effects. Our mission is to modify commonly used anticancer drugs (cytarabine, gemcitabine, topotecan, and others) to increase their selectivity through incorporation into lipid vehicles for ultrasound-mediated delivery. Currently our focus lies on topotecan—a topoisomerase inhibitor used in the treatment of solid-tumor cancers—onto which phospholipid tails were conjugated to form a prodrug that can be loaded into lipophilic environments without premature leaking. We hypothesize that topotecan is then released from the prodrug at the treatment site via non-specific esterase cleavage. 2T-T (“Two-Tailed Topotecan”) prodrug was successfully synthesized by conjugating phospholipid tails to the parent drug via Steglich esterification. The resulting compound was purified with chromatographic separation, producing a yield of 24%, and characterized with 1H and 13C Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (NMR). The prodrug was then loaded into liposomes and tested for biological activity via MTT cell proliferation assay. Biological effectiveness was verified by comparing 2T-T activity to the activity of parent topotecan. 2T-T showed comparable IC50 values to the parent drug at the nanomolar level, supporting our hypothesis that topotecan is released from 2T-T prodrug in its biologically active form at the cancer site. Future work includes further characterization as well as improvement of yield and biological activity. Drug modification such as this paves the way for future anticancer drugs with vastly improved safety and effectiveness.

title: Nanoparticle-Mediated Oral Delivery of GLP-1 for the Treatment of Diabetes
abstract: Diabetes is a tremendous health epidemic; it is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, affecting more than 30 million Americans [1]. The vast majority of cases are Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) which is characterized by insulin resistance and high blood sugar levels that can cause severe damage to the eyes, nerves, and organs, as well as increase the risk of cardiovascular disease [1]. A promising treatment for T2D utilizes incretin glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), which serves to enhance and promote insulin secretion while decreasing glucagon secretion by the pancreas [2]. Currently available treatments deliver GLP-1 via subcutaneous injections, which present complications including patient noncompliance, injection pain, and needle phobia [3]. Therefore, development of an oral delivery method would improve patient compliance and offer a safer, easier way to deliver drugs, improving outcomes and quality of life. We are developing a novel technique for oral delivery of GLP-1 using PLGA-PEG nanoparticles as a delivery device to remove the barriers caused by daily injections. The major challenges in administering oral therapeutics are protecting the drug against degradation in the harsh environment and fluctuating pH levels throughout the gastrointestinal tract, while facilitating drug delivery across the intestinal epithelial barrier layer. In this research, we synthesized and optimized the formulation of PLGA-PEG nanoparticles, then encapsulated GLP-1 in PLGA-PEG using a water-in-oil-in-water double emulsion. We characterized the size distribution of the GLP-1 loaded nanoparticles using Dynamic Light Scattering and tested the encapsulation efficiency and drug loading capacity using High Performance Liquid Chromatography. A Caco-2 epithelial cell monolayer was used to perform nanoparticle transport experiments. Transepithelial/transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) was performed to characterize the cell seeding density and optimize the monolayer’s readiness for the transport experiments. Nanoparticles were conjugated with fluorescence and permeability through the cell monolayer was tested. Based on these results, we will move forward with conjugating IgG antibodies onto the nanoparticles to facilitate transport across the intestinal epithelium. References: Type 2 Diabetes . title: Examining Siglec Signaling in Alzheimer’s Disease
abstract: Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) is a form of accelerated neurodegeneration and the most common form of dementia. There are currently few therapeutic options for AD patients, but the immune inflammatory response presents a potential therapeutic target once there is understanding of the underlying cellular signaling networks. We aimed to see if we could identify new targets in the immune system using an untargeted approach to signaling analysis. Using mass spectrometry to evaluate changes in protein phosphorylation of multiple mouse models of AD compared to aged matched controls, we have identified a Siglec signaling receptor that is activated on disease-associated microglial cells. We developed an expression system in BV2 cells with the wild type Siglec-F receptor, as well as inactive receptors where one or both cytoplasmic tyrosine residues have been mutated to phenylalanine. We assayed apoptosis to determine if altering functional tyrosine residues of these receptors will impact cell death and found that cells expressing wild type Siglec-F undergo significantly more apoptosis compared to those with mutated sites. We then treated BV2 cells with SHP099, an inhibitor of inflammatory transcription changes, to identify SHP-2-dependent and -independent signaling networks. This analysis identified other signaling proteins that could potentially be targeted to inhibit apoptosis. From these results, we see a potential to dissect signaling pathways activated by Siglec-F and target distinct phenotypic responses for inhibition. This approach could create a new avenue of therapeutic development for neuroinflammatory diseases.

title: Development of an in Vitro Model for Extravillous Trophoblast Invasion over a Gradient
abstract: It is currently difficult to establish the effect of external stimuli on extravillous trophoblast (EVT) invasion. Improper invasion of EVTs can cause problems with pregnancy, including the most common pregnancy complication, preeclampsia. Microfluidic devices are an option of modeling this early invasion; however, most trophoblast labs are not equipped to produce these devices through lithography. We are developing a device that will model the invasion of EVTs over gradients of maternal stimuli. We established novel methods to create the PDMS structure of the device, insert a 1 cm matrix to model the maternal decidua, establish a gradient that can be consistently confirmed, and track the movement of EVTs in 3 dimensions over time. This device will allow us to establish the effect of environmental factors, drugs, and other molecular regulators of placental development on EVT invasion.

title: Release of Griseofulvin from Spray-Dried Nanocrystal–Amorphous Solid Dispersions (HyNASDs): Impact of Surfactant
abstract: Over the last few decades, majority of the new chemical entities (NCEs) in the drug discovery pipeline are poorly-water soluble, and their slow dissolution turns out to be the rate-limiting step during intestinal absorption. Among different approaches to enhance bioavailability, two platform approaches have gained prevalence both in the scientific literature and marketed products: nanoparticle-based dosage forms (nanocomposites) and amorphous solid dispersions ( ASDs ). In the nanoparticle-based dosage form, dissolution rate is improved due to the dramatic increase in the surface area of the drug crystals via size reduction down to the nanoscale. On the other hand, amorphous form of the drug can offer significant enhancement in the extent–rate of dissolution due to its higher free energy and higher apparent solubility. A major shortcoming of drug nanocomposites as compared with amorphous solid dispersions (ASDs) is their limited supersaturation capability in dissolution media. Here, we prepared hybrid nanocrystal–amorphous solution dispersions (HyNASDs) in order to boost the drug release performance of traditional nanocomposites while elucidating the impact of a common anionic surfactant, sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), on drug release in dissolution tests. Wet-milled suspensions containing 1:1 to 1:5 GF:polymer mass ratios, with and without SDS, were spray-dried. Hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) and Soluplus (Sol) were used as suspension stabilizers and matrix-forming polymers. XRPD and DSC results suggest that nanocomposites and nanocomposites with notable amorphous GF (>10%), HyNASDs, were formed upon spray-drying. Redispersion of the spray-dried powders revealed the criticality of SDS in nanoparticle recovery from the nanocomposites/HyNASDs, which could be explained by GF wettability enhancement by SDS, as inferred from the modified Washburn experiment. Results from in vitro dissolution tests suggest that enhanced wettability with SDS and smaller spray-dried particle sizes led to faster GF release. For 100 mg GF dose (above thermodynamic solubility), Sol provided higher GF relative supersaturation, e.g. 250% for the HyNASDs (1:5 GF:Sol with SDS) vs. 30% for the nanocomposites (3:1 GF:Sol with SDS), than HPC (up to 50%) owing to Sol’s stronger intermolecular interactions–miscibility with GF and its kinetic solubilization–recrystallization inhibition of GF. SDS provided enhanced wettability, allowing for fast supersaturation from Soluplus-based HyNASDs (~300% within 20 min), while higher Soluplus loading led to higher supersaturation. Finally, this study demonstrates how drug release from traditional nanocomposites could be boosted upon incorporating a drug-miscible, solubilizing polymer with a low GF:polymer mass ratio and an anionic surfactant.

title: Supramolecular Filaments As Inhalable Drug Carriers for Lung Disease Therapies
abstract: Drug carrier systems that are capable of increased deposition, prolonged retention, and drug release in the lungs are extremely powerful in the treatment of diseases such as lung cancer, COPD, asthma, and tuberculosis. Supramolecular filaments (SFs) are a class of nanostructures formed by units such as peptide amphiphiles (PAs) ; peptides conjugated to alkyl chains and assembled through non-covalent forces. SFs can be “loaded” with therapeutic agents and controllably release these drugs upon filament disassembly. We take advantage of this technology to produce biocompatible PA-based drug carrier systems. Here, we provide key insights into PA design parameters necessary to deliver therapeutic agents effectively, a proof-of-concept in jet nebulization’s ability to effectively deliver drug-loaded supramolecular filaments, as well as a proposed mechanism of SF breakdown during nebulization.

title: Extraction of Biologically Produced Indigo Dyes
abstract: Indigo is a chemical that is used to dye clothing such as Levi Blue Jeans. The original method to produce dyes was extracting dyes from plants. However, this method took more than two weeks to ferment making it inefficient when the blue jean industry became popular. The current methods for producing clothing dyes are synthetic processes containing toxic and harmful steps. In order to reduce the health and environmental hazards, a biologically produced dye is being investigated as an alternative. In a previous study, it was found that a mutation in the enzyme, toluene ortho-monoxygenase, (TOM) of the bacteria Burkholderia cepacia would cause a change in color in rich media. The mutation A113V in the TOM enzyme results in the production of indigo. Using E. coli TG1, extraction and reduction methods are being investigated to develop a process for the production of indigo for use as a clothing dye. E. coli TG1 is grown for 48 hours with Isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) added at the 24-hour mark. The IPTG activates the production of indigo. Once cells are grown, the cells are pelleted and frozen to rupture the cells walls. Currently, chloroform is being used, but different solvents are being investigated for indigo extraction. Other solvents being studied include dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), tetrahydrofuran, and transcutol. Testing various solvents will help determine a chemical that decreases health and environmental hazards. After extraction, the dye is insoluble in water and must be converted into the leuco-form by a reduction mechanism. The leuco-form is water soluble and will adhere to the clothing. The current industrial method uses sodium dithionite which cannot be recycled, so other methods are being investigated such as biological and electrochemical methods. After the clothing is dyed, air oxidation converts the dye back to its original form, fixing it in the clothing.

title: Developing a Scalable Model for Optimum Growth in Stirred Tank Bioreactors
abstract: Stirred tank bioreactors are commonly used in many laboratory and industry applications. These reactors are often utilized in chemistry, biology, and pharmacy fields to examine important parameters. The most significant parameter of a bioreactor is the volumetric mass transfer coefficient (kLA) of oxygen. The kLA of oxygen is essential to measure efficiencies and scale-ups, and is widely affected by air flow rate, impeller type, impeller speed, and temperature. The experiment was first conducted in a 1L cylindrical glass reactor with a dished bottom. In this reactor, the kLA was measured using a gas cylinder that contains nitrogen and air. To test both the concentration and temperature of nitrogen and air, a dissolved oxygen and temperature probe were used. Nitrogen was measured by waiting for the oxygen concentration to decrease down to zero. After the oxygen concentration reached zero, air was measured until the dissolved oxygen completed 100% saturation. Depending on the amount of time is takes for nitrogen to reach zero and air to reach 100% saturation, different flow rates were adjusted so that the duration would run smoothly. Various types of impellers and impeller speeds were tested to see how the amount of time is affected as well. A 3L reactor was then repeated with same process that was done with the 1L reactor. This process was completed, and currently, the 3L bioreactor is being utilized to produce bacteria growth and cell culture. The bacteria being used in the process is Escherichia Coli due to its wide industrial use and fast-growing abilities. From using Escherichia Coli in the bioreactor with the various flow rates, impellers, and impeller speeds, we can see how fast the bacteria can absorb the oxygen and grow. To measure the concentration of the bacteria growth in the bioreactor, Optical Density (OD) measurements are recorded. This project is being tested in India as well by measuring bacteria growth and culture in larger reactors such as 5L and 7L. By doing these experiments on a smaller scale and a larger scale, we will be able to find the optimum parameters for a scalable model.

title: Application of Imaging Fluorescence Correlation Spectroscopy to Model Cell Membranes during Immunoreceptor Signal Transduction
abstract: The goal of this project is to understand the dynamic organization of the Rat Basophilic Leukemia (RBL) cell plasma membrane in its resting state. This is the first step in evaluating the extent of membrane remodeling that occurs during and after immunoreceptor signal transduction. We employed Imaging Fluorescence Correlation Spectroscopy (Imaging FCS) for this purpose. Imaging FCS is used to quantitatively measure diffusion modes of fluorescently labeled plasma membrane proteins. The changes of diffusion properties will be monitored as a function of physical and biochemical properties such as surface charge, post-translational modification, characteristics of transmembrane regions and availability of regulatory domains within the protein quaternary structures of membrane proteins. The observed dependence of membrane diffusion on these physico-chemical properties will eventually lead to a comprehensive understanding of the resting state of the RBL cell membrane.

title: Optimization of Carbon Delivery to Nannochloropsis Oceanica 849/10
abstract: Atmospheric carbon dioxide is a major contributor to global climate change. Nannochloropsis oceanica is a marine microalgae species showing viability as a large-scale carbon dioxide conversion method. Being a marine species, N. oceanica does not compete with agriculture for freshwater resources. This species also naturally has a high percentage of its cell weight dedicated to lipids, which can be refined into biodiesel fuel, thereby providing a renewable fuel source. In sea water, carbon dioxide is equilibrated between two forms, dissolved carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) and bicarbonate (HCO 3 - ). Bicarbonate has previously been determined as the primary carbon source for microalgae like N. oceanica . To maximize carbon dioxide conversion, the algae’s growth medium must have a high bicarbonate concentration, which requires a neutral to moderately basic pH. Experiments were conducted to determine the following: 1) standard growth curve of N. oceanica , 2) does N. oceanica prefer a bicarbonate source, and 3) baseline activity assays for commercially available carbonic anhydrase. Growth trials were run to determine if N. oceanica prefers either ammonium bicarbonate or sodium bicarbonate as a bicarbonate source. Sodium bicarbonate cultures had ammonium chloride added to maintain identical nitrogen concentrations. Total organic carbon (TOC) analysis showed that inorganic carbon (IC) concentrations, the combined concentration of carbonate and bicarbonate, decreased for cultures provided with ammonium bicarbonate. This decrease means N. oceanica consumed more bicarbonate. In contrast, the sodium bicarbonate/ammonium chloride cultures did not show a significant change in bicarbonate uptake. An activity assay was conducted on commercially available carbonic anhydrase for future reference on how factors such as temperature, acidity, buffered solution, and salinity affect enzymatic activity. These results are useful in determining how to improve algae-based carbon capture since carbonic anhydrase is a crucial component of the carbon concentrating mechanism in microalgae.

title: Metabolic and Regulatory Profiling of Caldicellulosiruptor Bescii reveals Promising Avenues for Lignocellulose Decomposition Optimization
abstract: Lignocellulose is the most abundant terrestrial carbon source, providing an attractive alternative to petroleum-based industrial chemicals. Harnessing the native cellulolytic ability of microorganisms is a promising avenue for industrial chemical production from renewable plant biomass; however, the need for pretreatment of lignocellulose limits its use in industrial processes. Caldicellulosiruptor bescii, a Gram-positive, anaerobic hyperthermophile growing optimally at 78°C, can deconstruct unpretreated lignocellulose and ferment both C5 and C6 sugars in a single step, making it a strong candidate for biologically mediated consolidated bioprocessing (CBP). While some chemicals such as ethanol have been demonstrated in C. bescii at moderate titers 1 , a deeper understanding of the physiology and regulatory networks of C. bescii is critical for the development of a scalable industrial process. Through metabolic reconstruction, biosynthetic pathways can be validated, prioritized, and optimized to redirect lignocellulosic sugars to target products. Here, we employed continuous culturing, transcriptome analysis, and in vitro characterization of regulatory proteins to investigate fermentation profiles, sugar uptake, and metabolic regulation. Fermentation profiles from continuous cultures of C. bescii on 5 g/L glucose or xylose at a dilution rate of 0.2 hr -1 show nearly the same theoretical yield of acetate (56.1% xylose, 55.7% glucose); however, glucose fermentation produces 4-fold more lactate. Because lactate production in C. bescii fermentation is due to buildup of H 2 , we investigated the influence of agitation rate on lactate production. Increased agitation rate from 150 rpm to 400 rpm led to a 10-fold reduction in lactate, a 1.7-fold increase in acetate, and exhaustion of carbon in the medium. By tuning the reactor operation, product yield and sugar consumption can be further controlled. Preliminary transcriptomics comparing glucose and xylose fermentation reveal upregulation of genes responsible for xylose transport and metabolism representing several distinct regulons, necessitating a robust metabolic reconstruction for sugar uptake and metabolism to account for crosstalk between pathways. Through in vitro characterization of C. bescii xylose metabolism regulators, further understanding of regulator binding and affinity will be determined, which is essential for the development of efficient, biologically mediated biofuel production. References: Williams-Rhaesa et al. Engineering redox-balanced ethanol production in the cellulolytic and extremely thermophilic bacterium, Caldicellulosiruptor bescii, Metabolic Engineering Communications, Volume 7, 2018

title: Engineering a Split Ubiquibody for Inducible Control of Protein Interface
abstract: Similar to humans throwing away trash, the cells in our body need to discard proteins that aren’t being used to prevent buildup. This process of protein degradation is accomplished through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (UPP), which tags the proteins to be degraded with a marker called ubiquitin (Portnoff, Stephens, Varner, DeLisa 2014). This pathway has been harnessed by several techniques to reduce levels of selectively targeted proteins by providing a method of eliminating proteins in the cell that are stable, but might be detrimental to cell function and life. Such techniques successfully enable degradation of targeted proteins, but are not modular, which requires an optimization for each new target protein. The goal of this project was to engineer a split ubiquibody, where the two ubiquibody domains (catalytic and binding) are expressed separately and dimerize in the presence of a chemical rapamycin. The results yielded a successful engineering of a split ubiquibody fused with either the FRB and FKBP protein. Before testing the dimerization of the two split complexes, the individual expression of each construct was tested to ensure that the individual complexes themselves could express well in mammalian cells. When testing these split ubiquibodies for expression using a Western Blot using both the FLAG and HIS tag, the complexes containing the binding domain expressed well consistently; however, catalytic domain had low expression indicating that the structure itself was not yet optimized for dimerization of the overall complex. To address this problem in the future, the complex with the catalytic domain is being redesigned with a linker and different orientations to improve stability and optimize expression.

title: Design Principles of Microparticle Backpacks for Control of Cellular Phenotype
abstract: An emerging platform for immunotherapy is the use of adoptively transferred cells of the innate immune system, such as macrophages, which can affect diseased tissues in an antigen-agnostic fashion. Macrophages display the most phenotypic plasticity out of any circulatory cell, which allows them to perform several related and often opposing biological functions, including promoting and suppressing inflammation, wound healing, and participating in host defense. However, the very plasticity that makes macrophages a versatile candidate for immunotherapy also hinders their ability to perform an intended function once transferred to the patient, as they can shift their phenotype in response to conflicting signals in the surrounding microenvironment. To address this issue, we have developed a disc-shaped microparticle “backpack” that is capable of attaching to macrophages and regulating their phenotype through the release of immunomodulatory cytokines. Backpacks are fabricated via microcontact printing of multiple layers of biodegradable polymers, which include a cell-binding layer and a cytokine-encapsulating layer (e.g., interferon-gamma, IFN-g). The thickness of the cytokine-encapsulating layer was tuned to balance stability and activity of IFN-g with microcontact-printing efficiency. The stiffness and size of the backpacks were confirmed with atomic force microscopy. Once fabricated, we show that the backpacks are able bind to the surface of primary murine-derived macrophages for at least 5 days. We also show that they release IFN-g over several hours to polarize the cells to which they are bound to a desired phenotype. Overall, the ability to control cellular phenotypes may allow for new cell-based therapies for a variety of immune-regulated conditions, including atherosclerosis, wound healing, and cancer.

title: The Role of dach1 in De Novo Formation of Collateral Arteries in the Uninjured Heart
abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD), is the leading cause of death in the US, accounting for 1 in 3 deaths annually. CAD occurs when coronary arteries (CAs) that supply the heart with oxygen become diseased. Collateral arteries, vessels that can interconnect CAs independent branches, can re-supply oxygen to the deprived muscle tissue, thereby maintaining heart function. Understanding the molecular factors involved in the development of the CAs and collaterals can lead to potential treatments for CAD. The transcription factor, DACH1, is necessary for CA development. In order to evaluate the role of DACH1 in collateral artery formation, we used an inducible transgenic murine line where DACH1 has been over-expressed (OE). Mice were induced at day 5 and processed for immunostaining at day 11 and week 12. iDISCO, a whole-mount immunolabeling clearing technique, and ImageJ were used to visualize, trace, and quantify the number of collaterals. We observed a slight decline in the number of collaterals in the OE vs WT at day 11 and expect this trend to repeat in the adults. Interestingly, a preliminary investigation on post-injury collateral formation yielded higher numbers in WT mice than OE. A qualitative analysis of the hearts suggest that the OE mice have more branches at the tips of the arteries. This indicates that the OE model may have a higher supply of oxygen to the heart and is a potential reason for the lower collateral count. In conclusion, this work brings us closer to understanding DACH1’s role in collateral artery formation.

title: Development of Wearable Cortisol Biosensor for Medical Application
abstract: Anxiety and depressive disorders alone affect over 400 million people and costs of over 1.5 trillion dollars per year. Although many people are affected, the psychiatric field still suffers from minimal understanding. There is a need to directly observe the essential biological nature of these disorders and move into objective, readily available indicators that can guide care. Cortisol, the body’s main stress hormone, is one of the most interesting biomarkers for many psychological disorders. There is a correlation between cortisol levels and several neurological disorders such as major depression, bipolar disorder, and anxiety. Cortisol levels can be measured using sweat, saliva, or blood. The current state of the art for measuring cortisol levels is phlebotomy, which uses blood samples, is invasive, and not applicable to tracking a patient continuously. The ability to continuously monitor cortisol levels could potentially give great insight into biological nature of these disorders and make way for a form of a diagnostic biological test which is currently nonexistent. It has been shown that the cortisol levels in sweat have a good correlation with those levels in blood. We believe that body sweat is a valuable source of biological information that can be used readily and monitored continuously. We chose commercial available metal oxide silicon field effect transistors (MOSFET) with an extended gate design as our sensor due to their high production speed, mechanical compatibility with skin, and low cost. Using competitive immunoassay, cortisol, a small molecule without charge removes the antibody from the surface of the extended gate displaying the large signal change necessary for our sensor. We are integrating this biosensing method into the extended gate MOSFET design due to the need to miniature the device for wearable application. Since one possible rout for sensing with extended gate structure is detecting the charges of the biomolecules, the research presented analyzes the effects of the buffer solutions Debye length, the scale which traveling charge carriers screen out electric field in conductors on the drift of the signal. The research presented will also detail the signal changes of the sensor as different MOSFETS with capacitances ranging from picofarad (pF) to nanofarad (nF) are paired with extended gate varying in surface area. By changing the surface area we can increase and decrease the total capacitance of the extended gate since the inherit capacitance is defined by the chemical functionalization itself.

title: Modeling the Amphiphilic Behavior of Quorum Sensing Signaling Molecules and Their Interactions with Lipid Bilayers
abstract: Quorum sensing is a bacterial communication process used to coordinate group behavior, such as the formation of antibiotic-resistant biofilms. Quorum sensing is controlled by the secretion and sensing a group of amphiphilic quorum sensing signaling molecules (QSSMs). In general, Gram-negative bacteria mainly use N -acyl homoserine lactones (AHLs), consisting of a polar homoserine lactone head group and a nonpolar aliphatic tail, as QSSMs. The urgency and severity of antibiotic resistance has led to interest in understanding the behavior of QSSMs in order to develop strategies to regulate bacterial communication. In this work, we developed a new protocol based on the conductor-like screening model for realistic solvation (COSMO-RS), in conjunction with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and quantum chemistry calculations, to investigate the amphiphilic behavior of AHLs by studying their self-assembly and their interactions with lipid bilayers. Atomistic MD simulations can determine the aggregation free energy and free energy of partitioning an AHL into a lipid bilayer with a large computational cost, whereas the new protocol incorporating COSMO-RS theory is at least 300 times faster than the MD simulation protocol with minor error. The results from the new protocol indicate that AHL head groups containing an additional 3-oxo group inhibit aggregation compared to their counterparts with only a single 3-oxo group in the head moiety, which is in agreement with the MD simulation results. The COSMO-RS results also indicate that longer aliphatic (more hydrophobic) tails facilitates aggregation and partitioning into a lipid bilayer, again in agreement with the MD simulation results. Comparison of the free energies for aggregation and partitioning indicates that aggregation is generally preferred, suggesting that aggregation may stabilize QSSMs in solution. Our faster COMSO-RS-theory-based protocol could be used as a high-throughput screening method for QSSM amphiphilic behavior and help guide the design of new AHL delivery techniques based on their membrane transport for better controlling the bacterial communication.

title: Evaluating Transport and Intracellular Uptake of a Protein Nanocarrier in 3-D Tumor Spheroids
abstract: The delivery of therapeutics into cells could open up many treatment options for various diseases such as cancer and neurological disorders, but these intracellular targets have been considered largely “undruggable” by small-molecule drugs that can penetrate the cell membrane. Delivery of antibodies directly to these targets would allow for more direct interaction with intracellular proteins, but intracellular antibody delivery remains an issue. To combat this, our lab has previously developed the Hex carrier, which can bind up to 3 antibodies per carrier and deliver them intracellularly in their functional form. Previously, I have shown via flow cytometry that HeLa cells treated with Hex-bound fluorescently labeled rabbit Immunoglobulin G (IgG Rb ) show a statistically significant increase in intracellular florescence compared to treatment with unbound IgG Rb . To further expand on previous studies of uptake in 2-D cell culture systems, the evaluation was extended to a 3-D tumor spheroid model. 3-D multicellular spheroids are very common models used to evaluate nanoparticle delivery, as they better mimic actual tumors as they would appear and behave in vivo. This allows for a more realistic assessment of nanoparticle transport and uptake at the tissue level. The intracellular uptake of fluorescent IgG Rb was assessed by flow cytometry to confirm that intracellular delivery is maintained in a complex, 3-D system. After being cultured and treated, the spheroids were digested with trypsin in order to break up the spheroid into individual cells for flow cytometry. Results of this analysis indicated positive fluorescence of the spheroids’ cells, indicating successful intracellular delivery despite the more complex system. This successful delivery of Hex in 3-D tumor spheroids provides further evidence of the improved delivery of antibodies by the Hex carrier. Future work will involve using confocal microscopy to evaluate transport of the Hex-antibody complex across the extracellular matrix into the interior of the spheroid, providing further support for Hex as an antibody delivery vehicle.

title: Introduction to Research through Protein Expression and Genetic Engineering of a Zwitterionic Amino Acid Fusion Protein
abstract: This project served as an introduction to the research process and the scientific method with hands-on application. Primarily aimed at cadets in their freshman and sophomore years. The vehicle for this project was protein expression in E. coli. The target protein was the nerve agent bio-scavenger, organophosphate hydrolyze (OPH). Previous studies demonstrated OPH’s broad substrate affinity for organophosphate compounds, such as, G-type nerve agents as well as its ability to enzymatically neutralize organophosphates (Liu, E. et al). Organophosphates are found in pesticides and nerve agents, and when exposed to the human body, inhibit the production of acetylcholinesterase causing overall action on the parasympathetic nervous system that leads to failure of neuron function (Liu, E. et al; Lerro, C. et al). Bio-scavengers like OPH have the potential to act as a protective protein. Obstacles to this include immunogenicity issues, short circulation time and low expression yield of genetically engineered fusion protein variants. Addressing these issues and building on previous studies, a genetically engineered, zwitterionic, amino acid, fusion protein was designed and initial expression results compared to the wild type OPH control.

title: Application of High-Throughput Screening Assay to Detect Glycosylated Proteins in Escherichia coli
abstract: Engineering of glycosylation pathways in bacterial cells has become an important tool for the development of microbe glyco-factories, conjugate vaccines, glycosylated outer membrane vesicles, and analyzing other roles glycosylated proteins play in various organisms. However, the encoding of genes that facilitate this post translational modification has been carried out in E. coli , an organism in which the enzyme is non-native. Thus, a robust and effective screening assay is necessary for initial detection of successfully secreted glycoproteins. A novel assay was developed for the high-throughput screening of N -glycosylation in Escherichia coli : GlycoSNAP ( glyco sylation of s ecreted N- linked a cceptor p roteins). However, since its development, a pathway for O -linked glycosylation has been engineered and successfully implemented in E. coli. O -linked glycoproteins have a much lower specificity for sugar substrates, thus facilitating a much wider range of potential application. Here, we describe the methodology of GlycoSNAP and its variable components, as well as its potential application in regards to O -glycosylation. GlycoSNAP has proven to be a successful high-throughput screening methodology, and is more affordable than its common counterpart, gel electrophoresis followed by Western blot. Its efficiency and modularity can, in principle, facilitate its application in a wide range of glyco-engineered variants.

title: Metabolic Engineering of Yeast for Production of Biopolymers
abstract: Bacteria are capable of making exopolysaccharide biopolymers like xanthan gums and hyaluronic acid, which can serve roles in food and health industries 1 . Making the sugar nucleotides that are precursors for xanthan gum and hyaluronic acid require purifying bacterial enzymes and use of cofactors that can make this process relatively inefficient and costly 2 . The goal of this research is to work towards making a yeast platform to serve as a whole cell catalyst that can make biopolymers such as hyaluronic acid. The first goal of this research was to overexpress the enzymes in the yeast Pichia Pastoris that can convert glucose into UDP-glucose, GDP-mannose, and UDP-glucuronic acid. Then, genes necessary for producing the biopolymers of interest from this increased pool of precursor sugar nucleotides can be added to the yeast DNA. Purification methods will then be used to purify the biopolymers made by the yeast.

title: Antimicrobial Activity of a Synthetic Polythiophene Oligomer
abstract: Cationic polythiophenes are used as antimicrobial compounds due to their ability to kill bacteria via the production of reactive oxygen species from the absorption of visible light. They are also able to damage negatively charged cell envelopes by selectively associating with them. This study demonstrates the ability of imidazolium- functionalized poly(3-hexylthiophene) (P3HT) to inactivate Gram-negative Escherichia coli under photolysis and dark conditions. Cell plating is used as a method to quantify cell death. The compound shows high levels of killing at 10 (μg/mL) polymer concentration for the Escherichia coli species after photoactivation as well as high levels of dark inactivation.

title: Transport of Human Milk Peptides Derived from in Vitro and In Vivo Digestion across a Model of the Human Intestinal Epithelium
abstract: Proteins in breast milk not only serve as nutrients for the infant, but also exert health beneficial properties that are necessary for the body’s physiological functioning. Proteins that contain chains of peptide sequences that are necessary for body functioning, beyond nutritional value, are known as bioactive peptides . There is still little knowledge on the effect of specific bioactive peptides on the body. Therefore, the objective of our study is to analyze the transport of peptides derived from in vitro and in vivo digestion of human milk proteins across a cell model of human small intestinal epithelium layer. Human milk was firstly under in vitro digestion and in vivo digestion in infants. The digested samples were collected and peptides were extracted from the sample. The extracted peptides were incubated with differentiated Caco-2 cell monolayer at the apical compartment of the insert. The peptides absorbed to the basolateral compartment were determined by mass spectrometry. This study will help assess Caco-2 permeability, along with which peptides will go into the bloodstream after digestion. For this study, it was hypothesized that human milk peptides released from in vitro digestion can be absorbed by human epithelium cell monolayer. Once we know more about the transport of proteins through digestion, the scientific community can further the understanding of how bioactive peptides work in the body. With the results of the experiment, there can be more research in discovering specific bioactive peptide sequences that can provide immune protection and reduce the risk of chronic diseases.

title: Designing Flavivirus Vaccines By Glycoengineering Protein Antigens
abstract: The goal of our work is to develop vaccines which provide broad protection against flaviviruses such as Zika and Dengue viruses. Zika outbreaks have been associated with a large increase in cases of microcephaly and Guillain-Barré syndrome. To date, there is no approved vaccine, antiviral drug, or other modality available to prevent or treat Zika – emphasizing the present need for a vaccine. Recent vaccine efforts have been focused on the Zika virus envelope protein (ZIKV E protein), which plays an important role in viral attachment and entry into host cells. The ZIKV E protein is composed of three spatially distinct structural domains (domain I (DI), domain II (DII), and domain III (DIII)). Previous research has shown that DIII is involved in receptor binding and elicits neutralizing antibodies. Researchers have recently characterized the epitopes for two distinct antibodies that target DIII: ZV-67 and ZV-2; only the epitope for ZV-67 was accessible in the context of the virion and only ZV-67 neutralized ZIKV in vivo . Thus, the goal of this study is to design an antigen that focuses the immune response on the ZV-67 epitope on DIII and effectively elicits antibodies that neutralize ZIKV. To achieve this goal, we are tuning the glycosylation of DIII. Glycans can be used as an antigen-modifier to direct the immune response away from or to a specific region of a protein. We hypothesize that shielding non-neutralizing epitopes on ZIKV DIII by glycosylation will direct the immune response towards the ZV-67 epitope to elicit more neutralizing antibodies. We also show how glycoengineering can be applied to other flaviviruses (i.e. Dengue).

title: Functionalization of Feed Spacers for Listeria Remediation in the Dairy Industry
abstract: Listeria Monocytogenes (LM) is a harmful foodborne pathogen that has the potential to contaminate industrial dairy processes. Pasteurization cannot completely prevent downstream recontamination, thus investigation into further sanitation methods is warranted. Quaternary ammonium compounds are of interest because the associated permanent positive charge promotes adhesion of negatively-charged bacterial membranes, along with subsequent leakage of cytoplasmic contents. Quaternary ammonium functional groups were integrated into the feed spacer material used in spiral wound membrane elements to treat LM recontamination. Unfortunately, European industrial regulations governing food processing may render the use of quaternary ammonium compounds impractical. Therefore, additional effort was devoted to the integration of phenolic compounds in the feed spacer material. Phenolic compounds induce enzyme deactivation and can contribute to degradation of bacterial cell walls. The immobilization of phenolic compounds on feed spacer material could offer an antimicrobial alternative to quaternary ammonium compounds when processing dairy products for the European market. In this investigation, polypropylene feed spacer mesh was modified to produce an antimicrobial material. The feed spacer was modified by three methods. In the first method, vinylbenzyl chloride was reacted with hexadecylamine and photopolymerized in the presence of the polypropylene mesh. The presence of the amine was assessed by Raman spectroscopy and dye analysis. Bacterial toxicity was assessed via biotesting with a surrogate bacterial strain, Lactobacillus plantarum . The second and third methods for feed spacer modification were designed to immobilize phenolic functional groups on the polypropylene material. Photopolymerization was performed in both instances, for a tyrosine-vinylbenzyl chloride mixture in the second method and a eugenol-butanol mixture in the third method. The presence of phenolic functional groups was assessed by aromatic ring-based dye characterization, and quantitative analysis was performed on the dye results via imaging analysis software.

title: DHL Family of Novel Anti-Cancer Drugs: Synthesis, Characterization and Activities
abstract: Cancer is the second most common cause of death in the United States with nearly 600,000 deaths a year. Novel anticancer drug researchers have been looking to naturally occurring molecules in order to combat this deadly disease. In particular, 2-amino pyrroles have been identified as very important biologically active scaffolds for the development of original anticancer, antibacterial, and antifungal drugs. Using aryl-substituted pyrrolines as a starting material, a novel anticancer scaffold, DHL, was successfully synthesized and characterized through NMR spectroscopy and X-Ray Crystallography. Changes of aryl aldehydes and sulfonamide were made to synthesize different derivatives, in order to characterize starting structure activity relationships. A total of twenty derivatives now exist within the DHL family. Each derivative was tested on cancer cell lines and activity was determined through MTT Assays. The compound with the best activity has been DHL-16, showing activity of 9.72µM.

title: Dispersion and Coating of Titanium Nitride Nanoparticles for Photothermal Therapy
abstract: Photothermal therapy is a minimally invasive cancer therapy strategy that damages targeted tumors by hyperthermia. Photothermal nanoparticles absorbs noninvasive near-infrared (NIR) light to elevate the temperature to ablate the targeted tumor cells. Titanium nitride (TiN) nanoparticles offer several advantages over conventionally used photothermal agent gold nanoparticles, such as strong absorption of light within the biological window (700-1000 nm), lower cost and biocompatibility. However, the main challenge to employ TiN nanoparticles for photothermal therapy is their colloidal instability in aqueous solution. They make aggregates larger than 200 nm in solution which is not suitable for delivering to the targeted cell. The goal of the project was to modify the surface of the TiN nanoparticles using polyethyelene glycol (PEG-40 Stearate) and liposomes to enhance their dispersibility in solution. Ultrasonic probe sonication was used to disperse the nanoparticles in deionized water and in 1x PBS (Phosphate Buffered Saline, PH 7.4) solution followed by centrifugation to remove large aggregates. The size of the nanoparticles was characterized using dynamic light scattering and the surface coating was confirmed using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy. The mean hydrodynamic diameter achieved for both liposomes coated and PEG coated nanoparticles in water were less than 200 nm. Additionally, liposome coating increases the colloidal stability of the nanoparticle’s dispersion in the aqueous solution. Unfortunately, neither the PEG-40 stearate or liposome coatings could prevent the aggregation of nanoparticle in PBS. Further research would be required to find suitable surface coating to effectively disperse the particles in a salt solution.

title: The Effect of Milling on Protein Enrichment of Yellow Pea during Electrostatic Separation
abstract: The standardized processes implemented for the separation of agro-material components (i.e. protein, starch and dietary fibers) are wet fractionation methods that involve the use of concentrated acids and/or alkali as well as energy-intensive dehydration step. In our Bioprocess Engineering Research Laboratory at Howard University, the focus is on developing a novel tribo-electrostatic separation process to effectively produce a protein-rich fraction of an agro-material in a water- and chemical-free environment. Our custom-built tribo-electrostatic separator encompasses of a fluidized bed, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) tribo-charging tube, and a rectangular separation chamber supplied with two copper-plate electrodes. For this study, yellow pea flours milled using two different milling types (i.e. pin and Ferkar milling systems) at two different milling intensities were first fluidized under the influence of pressurized air and then traveled through PTFE tribo-charging tube where protein particles were charged positively and attracted by the negatively-charged electrode plate. Our results highlight the importance of the milling types and intensities along with the air flow rates and electric field strengths for effective enrichment of yellow pea protein particles at their native states. Using the optimal milling and operating conditions, the original yellow pea protein content is increased by about 60% in the final collected protein fractions.

title: Investigation of Bacteriophage Encoded Toxins through Gene Analysis and Development of a Cell-Free Protein Production System
abstract: Prophage are viral sequences that have integrated into bacterial genomic DNA. Under certain conditions, these phage can be induced to replicate independently within the cell which allows the phage to disperse and infect other cells, thereby facilitating the horizontal spread of virulence and antibiotic resistance traits. We investigated the presence of a related group of prophage incorporated into the genome of Xanthomonas bacteria , a genus of common bacterial plant pathogens. We have designated this group of bacteriophage V-phage after the initially observed ‘Valentino’ and also for their potential role in virulence. We assessed the scope of bacterial strains possessing the phage in their genome and examined the conditions under which the prophage containing zot would enter the lytic cycle to begin actively replicating. Our aim is to characterize the specific proteins encoded for by the prophage, specifically focusing on the Xap toxin, which could be contributing to virulence in Xanthomonas and may be related to the zonula occludens toxin (zot) commonly produced by pathogenic strains of Vibrio cholerae . Toxins frequently impair bacterial growth during characterization experiments. For this reason, we are developing a cell-free approach to toxin production. This method, along with inducible cell-based systems, can be used to produce, purify, and study bacteriophage toxins such as Xap. Information regarding Xap and the group of V-phage could aid in understanding the role that bacteriophages and related molecules play as reservoirs of virulence factors in both plant and mammalian pathogens. Furthermore, future work to characterize Xanthomonas gene expression and related phage could aid in the creation of target-specific antimicrobials for common plant pathogens.

title: Comparison of Different Methodologies for Rapid GC/MS Analysis of Volatile Organic Acids in Fermentation Media
abstract: The volatile fatty acids (VFAs) acetic, propionic and butyric acid have significant inhibition effects on activated sludge microbial consortia. Inhibition has been shown to be the highest at total VFA concentrations of 10 g/L and 20 g/L. A rapid easy to use method for the determination of VFAs was developed with no or limited sample preparation to ensure sample integrity. Liquid Chromatography (LC) has been the standard for the analysis of VFAs and requires filtration prior to analysis to remove fermentation cells and other by-products that could foul the LC column resulting in downtime and expense of column replacement. To avoid this, we have developed two methods using Gas Chromatography (GC) for a rapidly reduced sample productive alternative. The first is a Liquid-Liquid Direct Extraction with phase separation in an autosampler vial with the autosampler drawing sample from the organic phase. The other technique utilizes Solid-Phase Microextraction (SPME) technology. The sample is placed directly into a GC vial and the SPME fiber extracts and injects VFAs into GC inlet. Comparisons of the two techniques compared to traditional LC method showed the Direct Liquid-Liquid provided the lowest detection limits. The SPME detection of VFAs was shown to have slightly higher detection limits but requires no sample preparation as compared to the other techniques. Linearity of VFAs and chromatography examples will be discussed.

title: High Temperature Measurements of Multicomponent Foods
abstract: Low-water-activity and low-moisture foods are generally considered safe due to the inability of microorganisms to grow under such conditions. Recently, there have been a surprising number of recalls on low-water-activity foods due to pathogens such as Salmonella agona . To understand this issue, we investigated the dependence of water activity on S. agona inactivation in multicomponent (carbohydrate, protein, fat) food systems. Initial results indicated that a high-fat multicomponent food requires a longer time for complete S. agona inactivation. We conducted a follow-on study to confirm water activity at high temperatures and the starting moisture contents of each multicomponent food system using a series of moisture content and water activity measurements. To date, the initial and current data have been consistent across the studies. These results imply that further studies are required to understand how different types of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats will differ while undergoing S. agona inactivation.
